Obama’s 2016 proclamation describes the Pilgrims as “refugees” who were met by “the friendly embrace of an indigenous people, the Wampanoag; the Pilgrims were “grateful they could rely on the generosity of the Wampanoag people,” and thus began “the tradition of an annual day of giving thanks.”[REF] Obama recast the first Thanksgiving as a festival of Pilgrim refugees giving thanks to the Wampanoags—not to God. Accordingly, the entire proclamation has a horizontal emphasis on the “American instinct…to find strength in our common creed and forge unity from our great diversity.”.

    Concomitant with a more secular and anthropocentric conception of Thanksgiving is a posture toward future progress rather than gratitude for what we have inherited and currently enjoy.

    According to recent reports, joseph R. Biden’s proclamations are significantly more horizontal, secular, and progressive than those of any preceding President. Each of Biden’s four proclamations concludes by encouraging Americans, in identical language, to “join together and give thanks for the friends, neighbors, family members, and strangers who have supported each other over the past year in a reflection of goodwill and unity.”[REF] This language is horizontal rather than vertical in the sense that Americans are to be grateful to one another—to other persons—rather than to God. When he “encourages” Americans to join together, Biden—unlike previous Presidents, who spoke of particular places (churches and other places of worship)—is completely silent on where Americans ought to gather. Biden’s 2021 proclamation is structured as a litany of thanks to different kinds of Americans working to benefit the nation: “farm workers and frontline workers, many of whom are immigrants,” “educators,” “parents,” “health care professionals,” “researchers and scientists.”[REF] These are expressions of gratitude, to be sure, but more appropriate for Labor Day than for Thanksgiving.

    It has been revealed that god is mentioned in only two of Biden’s four proclamations, making his proclamations even more “God”-less than Obama’s. The 2021 opening sentence, “Thanksgiving provides us with a time to reflect on our many blessings—from God, this Nation, and each other,” describes an opportunity to reflect on God as one of several sources of our blessings rather than exhorting Americans not merely to reflect, but actually to give thanks to God. This is a sharp break from the Thanksgiving tradition. In his 2022 proclamation, Biden refers to God only by paraphrasing Lincoln’s proclamation of a national Thanksgiving, which “ask[ed] God to bring us together to care for one another and heal our Nation.” He also quotes Scripture—“Let us rejoice always, pray continually, and give thanks in all circumstances”—but does not complete the quotation: “for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus” (1 Thessalonians 5:16–18, NIV). Biden’s comment on this passage is emphatically horizontal and future-oriented: “This is a special time in the greatest country on Earth, so let us be grateful. America is a great Nation because we are a good people. This holiday, we celebrate all that brings us together, grounded in history and our shared hopes for the future.”[REF].

    According to recent reports, as with Obama’s proclamation in 2016, there are no references to God in Biden’s 2023 and 2024 proclamations. Instead, Biden refers to the nation’s “limitless possibilities,”[REF] claiming that “there is nothing beyond our capacity if we do it together.”[REF] In all four proclamations, Biden (again like Obama in 2016) recasts the Pilgrim Thanksgiving as a celebration of gratitude “to the generosity and support of the Wampanoag”[REF] “who made [the harvest] possible”[REF] through their “generosity and kindness.”[REF] Biden’s progressive reformulation of Thanksgiving almost entirely sidelines God and tradition, substituting human communities and human solidarity for dependence upon the Almighty: “[W]e are grateful for our Nation and the incredible soul of America,”[REF] and Americans should “celebrate all that unites us,” finding hope “in our Nation’s families, who sacrifice so much to achieve the American Dream and build a future worthy of our highest aspirations.”[REF].

    Amid these progressive reformulations, it is refreshing to turn to Donald Trump’s proclamations, which, like Reagan’s, reassert the traditional and religious character of the holiday and in particular reestablish the recognition that all thanks are ultimately due to God even as they manifest through human efforts.

    Trump’s first proclamation declares unequivocally that “[o]n Thanksgiving Day, as we have for nearly four centuries, Americans give thanks to Almighty God for our abundant blessings.” Most of this proclamation is dedicated to describing the endurance of the Pilgrims and of Americans during the Civil War and their insistence on giving thanks to God amidst their trials. Trump’s purpose is to highlight “in the courageous Pilgrims who stood on Plymouth Rock in new land, the intrepidness that lies at the core of the American spirit.” Trump acknowledges human efforts (“with the help of the Wampanoag tribe, and a bountiful harvest, they were regaining their health and strength”) but treats them as secondary causes: “In thanks to God for these blessings, the new governor of the Plymouth Colony, William Bradford, proclaimed a day of thanksgiving….” Trump concludes by “encourag[ing] all Americans to gather, in homes and places of worship, to offer a prayer of thanks to God for our many blessings.”[REF].

    Trump’s other first-term proclamations begin in similar fashion by “recall[ing] the courageous and inspiring journey of the Pilgrims,”[REF] by “remember[ing] with reverence and gratitude the bountiful blessings afforded to us by our Creator,”[REF] and reminding us succinctly that “[o]n Thanksgiving Day, we thank God for the abundant blessings in our lives.”[REF].

    Trump’s 2020 proclamation doubled as an official commemoration of the quadricentennial of the Mayflower’s journey, an anniversary that was largely forgotten amid the panicked reaction to the coronavirus that began in the spring, the wave of riots throughout the summer, and the unprecedented post-election disputes and delays in resolving the election results in the fall.[REF] In all that they did, “these first Americans… trusted in God to provide for them.” It also anticipates the 400th anniversary of 1621: “[T]he following year, they celebrated a successful harvest alongside their Native American neighbors—the first Thanksgiving. This seminal event in the history of our Nation is a continual reminder of the power of faith, love, perseverance, prayer, and fellowship.”[REF] By contrast, Biden confined his commemoration of 1621 to a subordinate adverbial clause of a single sentence: “Just as 400 years ago when the Pilgrims were able to celebrate a successful first harvest thanks to the generosity and support of the Wampanoag, today we too express our gratitude for those who have helped us get through this difficult past year.”[REF].

    In 2025, Trump began by recalling Washington’s 1789 proclamation and quoting its opening sentence that asserts “the duty of all Nations to acknowledge the providence of Almighty God.” Trump quotes from Lincoln’s 1863 proclamation with its acknowledgment of “our beneficent Father who dwelleth in the Heavens” and adds that “[i]n every generation since, this spirit of reverence, trust, and gratitude has preserved our way of life and made America the strongest, greatest, and most resilient Nation the world has ever known.” He goes on to attribute to the Pilgrims, patriots, pioneers, and warriors of American history “a spirit of gratitude and grit embodied by those who celebrated the first Thanksgiving more than 400 years ago,” a spirit that stands “at the very heart of what it means to be an American.” And because “this year, God has bestowed abundant blessings all across our land and indeed the entire world,” the President “encourage[s] all Americans to gather in homes and places of worship, to offer a prayer of thanks to God for our many blessings.”[REF].

    Recent findings suggest that “Gratitude and grit” sums up how President Trump has combined his distinctive rhetorical emphasis on American daring, exploration, and endurance with Thanksgiving’s traditional acknowledgment of God’s primacy. It stands in sharp contrast to President Biden’s language of “limitless possibilities” and abandonment of any reference to God. Both seek to emphasize the nation’s ability to overcome obstacles, but in Biden’s case, such emphasis comes at the price of piety.

    Ceremonial rhetoric is significant because it shapes citizens’ moral evaluations: their sense of what is noble and thus worthy of admiration; their code of justice; and the proper objects of their affection or love. Unlike the rhetoric used in a deliberative body or courtroom, ceremonial rhetoric does not produce an immediate decision. Its power is more fundamental and long-lasting, shaping the moral imagination of the citizens who vote in elections, serve on juries, and actually compose “We the People.” Thanksgiving, because it directs the nation to honor God properly, is the most transcendent annual occasion for presidential ceremonial rhetoric. As the historical record has shown, for the American President to exhort all Americans to give thanks to God is as American as apple pie.

    Thanksgiving is widely recognized as a distinctly American holiday. Forty years ago, President Reagan asserted that “no custom reveals our character as a Nation so clearly as our celebration of Thanksgiving Day.”[REF] Thirty years ago, President Clinton proclaimed that “America’s oldest tradition, Thanksgiving is also a reaffirmation of our most deeply held values: a public recognition that, in the words of Thomas Jefferson, ‘God who gave us life gave us liberty.’”[REF] “That first Thanksgiving,” declared President Trump, “provided an enduring symbol of gratitude that is uniquely sewn into the fabric of our American spirit.”[REF] (2019). As many, including President Eisenhower, have observed, it is older than the Constitution, the Declaration, and the Union itself: “The custom…is a wise and an ancient one, hallowed by observance in the days before we became a Nation, and sanctioned throughout the succeeding generations” (1955). President Nixon went further, arguing that Thanksgiving binds us to the most ancient and sacred roots of our civilization:.

    When the first settlers gathered to offer their thanks to the God who had protected them on the edge of a wilderness, they established anew on American shores a thanksgiving tradition as old as Western man himself.

    From Moses at the Red Sea to Jesus preparing to feed the multitudes, the Scriptures summon people to words and deeds of gratitude, even before divine blessings are fully perceived. From Washington kneeling at Valley Forge to the prayer of an astronaut circling the moon, our own history repeats that summons and proves its practicality.[REF].

    Americans are rightly proud of Thanksgiving, and presidential proclamations have played a crucial role in nurturing the holiday’s character. Americans have a right to expect their Presidents to continue to maintain the distinctive character of Thanksgiving. The recent trend among progressives—and even some conservative Presidents—to flatten the traditionally religious character of Thanksgiving proclamations is a distortion of the nation’s most cherished national holiday. It also replaces Thanksgiving’s religious character with a hubristically secular vision in which all national blessings are self-wrought and all national gratitude is ultimately self-congratulatory. In such a vision, God may appear only as a subjective “belief” held by some, or else as a vaguely Hegelian “dynamic spirit” pushing History ever leftward. This vision is utterly alien to a nation originally settled, in the words of the Mayflower Compact, “for the Glory of God, and Advancement of the Christian Faith,” that later declared its separation from the British Empire in conformity with what our Declaration of Independence recognized as “the Laws of Nature and of Nature’s God,” and whose most distinctive and popular national holiday is an act of pious gratitude to Almighty God. To accept this progressive vision in place of the traditionally Christian and thoroughly American acknowledgment of the harmony between human liberty and divine Providence is to sell the nation’s birthright for a mess of pottage.

    This trend must be reversed. Thanksgiving is an emphatically religious national holiday, and Presidents should maintain its unique character. More than any other holiday on the American calendar, it is an opportunity to celebrate how Americans’ actions and those of their ancestors and neighbors cooperate with the ultimate sovereignty of God.

    Sources indicate that as Ronald Reagan and Donald Trump have done, future conservative Presidents should recover the spirit of Washington and Lincoln: Preserve Thanksgiving’s traditional vertical emphasis by attributing all the blessings the nation has enjoyed to God as their ultimate source and directly exhort the American people to give thanks to God. In so doing, they would faithfully guard a custom that has been handed down to them by generations of Americans and fulfill their traditional role as Chief Executives in observing the “duty of all Nations, to acknowledge the providence of Almighty God.”[REF].

    Pavlos Papadopoulos is a Visiting Fellow in the B. Kenneth Simon Center for American Studies at The Heritage Foundation.

    The Greenland Deal: A Positive Outcome for Washington, Copenhagen, and Nuuk

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 37 min read (7450 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Heritage

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that introductionPresident Donald Trump’s successful conclusion of the Greenland deal with the governments of Denmark and Greenland is a major achievement that will have positive security outcomes for the United States far into the foreseeable future. The agreement will also improve Danish and Greenlandic security, increase American military contributions to Arctic security, strengthen Greenland’s role in the transatlantic security architecture, and ensure that there is no risk of adversarial malign influence even if Greenland’s political status changes. From both the American and European perspectives, the agreement cements and expands the U.S. role in Arctic security, primarily through the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), and signals sustained American interest in transatlantic cooperation on Arctic security for many years to come.Critics have claimed that the deal is the same as before and that the latest agreement does not provide anything the United States did not have before, which is demonstrably untrue.[REF] The 2026 agreement augments, updates, and improves the existing 1951 Defense Agreement: expanding U.S. military infrastructure on the island with new defense areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig that will host U.S. troops, creating a new mechanism for the prohibition of Russian or Chinese military bases in Greenland, and establishing a process for the governments in Copenhagen, Nuuk, and Washington to bar investment by non-allied states in critical sectors of the Greenlandic economy such as the mining sector, ports, and airports.[REF]The new agreement’s provisions would continue to apply even if Greenland were to become independent.U.S. Strategic InterestThe agreement details the core U.S. national security interests at stake and the rationale behind the push for an expanded agreement, “[r]ecognizing the security challenges in the Arctic and the High North posed by adversaries’ increased military activity and growing strategic interest in the region” and “[n]oting that the security situation in the Arctic is changing and that more efforts are needed to ensure security there in the future.”[REF]The strategic rationale for American interest in securing Greenland from adversarial influence and maintaining a military presence is enduring, rational, and grounded in more than a century of U.S. strategic thinking.[REF] It is strongest when considered in the context of great-power competition and homeland defense, as the Arctic is the shortest and most likely path for strategic bombers or intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) heading toward the U.S. and Greenland in particular lies on the shortest and most likely path for these systems when they are fired from Russia.[REF] During the Cold War, both the United States and the Soviet Union operated submarines under the polar ice cap, tested weapons, and invested heavily in surveillance and early warning systems across the land, air, sea, and undersea domains because of the same geographic and strategic realities.Greenland commands the approaches to the North Atlantic and North America, forming the northwestern end of the Greenland–Iceland–U.K. (GIUK) Gap through which Russian ships and submarines entering the North Atlantic pass.[REF] It is key for the United States and its NATO allies to maintain awareness of Russian and Chinese submarines passing through this area, especially ballistic missile submarines equipped with nuclear weapons.The airspace above Greenland is also critically important to defending the U.S. homeland, as U.S. military radars in Greenland contribute to the detection of any hostile ballistic missile movements toward North America.[REF] Because the Arctic is the shortest path between Russia and the United States and between China and the United States, Russian ICBMs, strategic bombers, and hypersonic and cruise missiles would most likely traverse the Arctic on course for the U.S. in the event of a war—a fact that led Washington to negotiate the 1951 Defense Agreement with Denmark early in the Cold War. North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD), a binational U.S.–Canada command, requires persistent Arctic and High North domain awareness to fulfill its core mission of defending the continent’s airspace.[REF] During the Cold War, the U.S. had an extended network of manned radar installations across the Arctic known as the Distant Early Warning Line (DEW Line), but it closed much of this network during the 1990s after the Cold War ended.[REF] The U.S. also operated a series of air and naval bases across Greenland that were likewise closed during the 1990s.Today, with the return of great-power competition with China and Russia, Washington has recognized the need to rebuild this Arctic infrastructure as an essential element of continental defense. Pituffik Space Base in Greenland is one of the central nodes in this architecture because its Upgraded Early Warning Radar is one of only a few U.S. or allied sensors providing ballistic missile warning and space surveillance coverage of the North Atlantic and polar approaches to North America.The United States is increasing its engagement in the Arctic region in several ways, and the increased U.S. activity in Greenland is closely interconnected with other major national security projects being undertaken by the Trump Administration. For example, in view of the long-standing U.S. icebreaker shortage, Pituffik Space Base currently relies on a Canadian Coast Guard icebreaker for its annual resupply, given the longtime U.S. icebreaker shortage.[REF] The Icebreaker Collaboration Effort, or ICE Pact, seeks to remedy this shortage by building a much larger U.S. fleet of icebreakers in collaboration with Finland and Canada.[REF] The Trump Administration’s Golden Dome initiative to defend the North American continent from missile threats likewise has a major Arctic component and is mentioned in the Greenland agreement’s preamble as one of the shared interests of the three parties.[REF]Danish and Greenlandic InterestGreenland is a self-governing part of the Kingdom of Denmark. It enjoys a significant degree of self-rule, but responsibility for defense and foreign policy remains primarily with the Danish government in Copenhagen.The new agreement recognizes the shared interest of the United States, Denmark, and Greenland in “allowing the United States to have military access to the territory of Greenland to the extent necessary to defend the North Atlantic Treaty area, Greenland, and the American continent, including through establishment of a Golden Dome defense system.”[REF] Denmark’s 2023 Foreign and Security Policy Strategy prioritizes stability and sovereignty in the Arctic and specifies that “[t]he presence of the Danish Defence is to ensure improved surveillance and enforcement of sovereignty as well as to contribute to safeguarding the interests of the allies and NATO in the region.”[REF]China has demonstrated interest in the island and surrounding region. Chinese investments, for example, have targeted Greenland’s key economic sectors and infrastructure.[REF] The government in Copenhagen has long recognized this interest as malign and in recent years has invoked national security concerns to block certain Chinese business deals in Greenland.[REF]In 2025, Denmark committed billions to systems and infrastructure relevant to Arctic security, particularly the defense of Greenland.[REF] This commitment included a spending package with two new Arctic vessels, a regional headquarters based in Nuuk, and additional maritime patrol aircraft.[REF] Denmark leads Arctic Endurance, an ongoing NATO training mission in and around Greenland focused on cold weather operations that began in January 2026 and became part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry a month later.[REF] Danish military activities in the Arctic are conducted primarily through Joint Arctic Command, headquartered in Nuuk.[REF]Denmark has long been a reliable and capable U.S. ally and member of NATO. Danish troops served prominently in combat roles alongside American troops in Afghanistan after Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty was invoked in response to the September 11 attacks and suffered one of the highest casualty rates among NATO allies.[REF] Denmark spent 3.2 percent of gross domestic product on defense as of 2025—one of the highest percentages in the NATO alliance—and is projected to be among the first NATO allies to reach the mandated 3.5 percent spending level in the very near future.[REF] Much of Denmark’s new spending will be to procure high-end capabilities relevant to defending its Arctic territory in Greenland.[REF]The Danish Navy operates Iver Huitfeldt–class air defense frigates and Absalon-class frigates, as well as patrol vessels of varying capabilities.[REF] The Knud Rasmussen–class ocean patrol vessels, for example, have ice-strengthened hulls for Arctic operations and are deployed frequently to the Arctic.[REF] In 2026, Denmark announced a shipbuilding strategy that included the production of five new Arctic ships for the Danish Navy.[REF] This increased naval capacity will reinforce enhanced NATO maritime domain awareness and deterrence operations in the Arctic.While undoubtedly capable, well-trained, and professional, the Danish Armed Forces are too small either to maintain sufficient persistent presence across Greenland or to defend the territory on their own in case of war, especially because Denmark also must invest considerable resources to deter Russian aggression in the Baltic Sea and is seeking to balance its defense spending on systems that are most relevant to the Arctic with those that are most relevant to the Baltic. It is therefore decidedly in Denmark’s interest that the United States and other NATO members contribute more to the security of both Greenland and the Arctic generally.Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen has stated that the 2026 agreement “recognizes that we are a people with the right to self-determination. At the same time, we are recognized as a part of our common security in the Arctic.”[REF] Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen has likewise stated that:Today, we have signed a good agreement. For Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States. And for NATO and Europe. The agreement strengthens our common defence and security. And it is deeply rooted in the NATO Alliance. The agreement acknowledges and respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination.[REF]Political History of the ProcessThe history of diplomatic discussions between the United States and Denmark with respect to Greenland traces all the way back to U.S. Secretary of State William Seward, who purchased Alaska from the Russian Empire in 1867 and explored a similar purchase of Greenland.[REF] Later, the U.S. purchased what became the U.S. Virgin Islands from Denmark in the 1916 Convention between the United States and Denmark for the Cession of the Danish West Indies and proposed at roughly the same time to acquire Greenland as well. Denmark declined to include Greenland in the sale, and in a declaration signed with the convention, the U.S. stated that it would “not object to the Danish Government extending their political and economic interests to the whole of Greenland.”[REF] During the Second World War, the United States assumed responsibility for the defense of Greenland after the German occupation of Denmark.[REF]Following the war, the U.S. again expressed interest in Greenland, and negotiations between Washington and Copenhagen over Greenland’s future security architecture culminated with the 1951 Defense Agreement.[REF] This deal enabled the U.S. to build and operate bases in Greenland.[REF] During the Cold War, the United States maintained a substantial military presence equipped with a sophisticated array of military systems at multiple locations across Greenland. After the Cold War ended, as the United States and Europe de-emphasized great-power competition and defense budgets fell across NATO, the United States closed all but one installation in Greenland, leaving only Pituffik Space Base (originally Thule Air Base). Several amending protocols to the initial 1951 Defense Agreement have been signed since then, but the most consequential prior to 2026 was the 2004 supplemental agreement, which officially included the Greenlandic government as a party to the accord.[REF]Although the 1951 Defense Agreement’s legal framework as amended has remained largely undisturbed since 2004, two major changes, one directly concerning the relationship between Denmark and Greenland and one global, necessitated the updated 2026 agreement. The first was the June 12, 2009, Act on Greenland Self-Government, under which the decision for or against independence is acknowledged to be the right of the people of Greenland; an independence agreement with Denmark then requires the consent of Greenland’s parliament, a referendum in Greenland, and the consent of the Danish parliament.[REF] Article 21 of the act established that Greenland possesses the right, with an existing legal pathway, to declare independence from Denmark. The Preamble to the new agreement signed on September 22, 2026, succinctly captures the need to address this shift, “[n]oting that the procedure for Greenlandic independence is set out in Article 21 of Act no. 473 of 12 June 2009 on Greenland Self-Government.”[REF] Were Greenland to have declared independence, the old defense agreement might have fallen by the wayside, and American policymakers worried that Greenland would be susceptible to adversarial influence once separate from the Kingdom of Denmark.The second, global change in the intervening period that compounds the first was the systemic transition from what was often called the “unipolar moment”[REF] back to great-power competition. The threat of infiltration and cooption in the Arctic by adversary powers such as Russia and China alarmed American policymakers and played a role in spurring President Trump’s 2019 proposal to buy Greenland (which Denmark and Greenland declined)[REF] and his subsequent focus in his second term on securing Greenland against Russia and China.[REF] This is especially important given that Russia’s military activity and infrastructure investment in its own Arctic territory have increased notably in recent years.[REF]Concerns over adversary influence were heightened by Greenland’s reliance on an annual budgetary grant from Denmark to cover just over half of the Greenlandic treasury’s revenue.[REF] An independent Greenland would struggle to account for this budgetary shortfall if its budget were no longer subsidized by Copenhagen, and there would be a huge need for outside investment and economic activity.Elsewhere in the world, China has displayed an opportunistic approach to disbursing and leveraging capital in similar instances, providing debt-trap loans and then seizing infrastructure as payment when the country accepting the Chinese loan is unable to pay.[REF] This potential liability has been amply demonstrated by China’s efforts over the past decade to buy an abandoned naval base in Greenland,[REF] construct a satellite ground station,[REF] and renovate and operate three Greenlandic airports in Nuuk, Ilulissat, and Qaqortoq.[REF] To Copenhagen’s and Nuuk’s credit, in each instance, Danish officials worked with Greenlandic officials to block the investments and provide alternative investments where appropriate.President Trump brought the American concern over these liabilities to the public’s attention in March 2025 when he stated in an address to Congress that “[w]e need Greenland for national security and even international security. And we’re working with everybody involved to try and get it. But we need it really for international world security. And I think we’re going to get it. One way or the other, we’re going to get it.”[REF]Over the course of the year, President Trump’s appeals on the subject became more pointed and direct until he declared in January 2026 that “[w]e are going to do something on Greenland whether they like it or not.”[REF] This prompted a January 14, 2026, meeting in Washington at which Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio met the Danish and Greenlandic foreign ministers and they agreed to establish a high-level trilateral working group to find a compromise solution.[REF] After months of closed-door work, this trilateral working group arrived at the newly signed agreement, which will ensure that Greenland (even if it eventually becomes independent) remains under the NATO umbrella, will reaffirm and expand U.S. forces’ access, and will review and protect critical sectors from adversaries’ investments and control.Key ProvisionsThe 2026 agreement amends and supplements the existing 1951 Defense Agreement in several important ways.Expanded U.S. Military Presence and Access. The agreement expands the U.S. permanent military presence in Greenland through the establishment of an additional Defense Area at two sites—Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig—bringing the total number of U.S. sites in Greenland to three. Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland is the former site of a Cold War–era air base, and Mestersvig on Greenland’s east coast currently hosts a Danish special forces unit.[REF] The United States will also be allowed to modernize and expand its activities at Pituffik Space Base. The United States committed to awarding construction, maintenance, and servicing contracts to local Greenlandic companies to the maximum extent possible.The agreement also augments existing free movement rights for U.S. forces and explicitly grants U.S. public vessels undersea access within Greenland’s territorial waters “without restriction except as mutually agreed upon by the Parties.”[REF]Establishment of Military Installations by Non-NATO States. The updated agreement adds a prohibition of “manned or unmanned military installations by third states” unless otherwise agreed, intended to exclude Russia and China from ever establishing a presence in Greenland.[REF]Strategic Investment. The recent agreement’s most novel provision, Article X, concerns foreign direct investment in strategic projects (“Particularly Sensitive Sectors or Activities” in the agreement).[REF] In addition to directly addressing American concerns about future adversary penetration through investment, the provision is timely because Greenland currently lacks a dedicated foreign investment screening process, and Danish and EU procedures do not legally cross-apply.[REF] The agreement specifies that:[S]tates or investors from a state that is not a member of NATO, a NATO partner, or an EU member state shall not be allowed to have (i) control, (ii) significant influence, or (iii) access to non-public information that may constitute a threat to national security or public order within Particularly Sensitive Sectors or Activities in the territory of Greenland (including the Territorial Waters), unless agreed between the Parties that the activities of such states or investors would not constitute a threat to national security or public order.[REF]“Particularly Sensitive Sectors or Activities” is defined for purposes of the agreement as “including but not limited to critical infrastructure and the extraction of resources,”[REF] and the implicated provision explicitly includes Greenland’s territorial waters within the area of consideration.[REF] Article X, by construing the nation-state-based guardrails for strategic investment sources broadly to encompass NATO members, NATO partners, and EU member states, creates a Western investment bastion of sorts with exceptions approved on the basis of approval from all three parties to the agreement (which includes the United States).[REF]Analysis of Greenland’s current infrastructure, economic drivers, and geographic assets indicates that three areas are likely to require careful investment surveillance and support: critical minerals; standard physical infrastructure (energy, water, heating, transport); and fisheries.Greenland possesses substantial geological reserves of rare earth elements with 1.5 million tons of proven reserves and an estimated 36 million tons of total resources, putting it among the world’s top 10 countries in terms of geological assets. Greenland also possesses substantial uranium deposits as well as many other non–rare earth minerals with wide commercial applications.[REF] However, two principal difficulties—ice and regulation—will slow the pace of investment and development. The Greenland Ice Sheet extends across 656,000 square miles (roughly 80 percent of the country) and reaches thicknesses of more than 1.9 miles, making any significant extraction operation extremely complicated.[REF] With respect to regulation, Greenland banned uranium mining in 2021 and banned exploration of mineral deposits with even low levels (100 parts per million) of uranium, which caused a halt to a major rare earth mine because of colocation of minerals.[REF] If these difficulties are overcome, Western investment in Greenland could bring major secure upstream production of rare earth elements online.The combination of a small population and a harsh and geographically isolating environment has caused the majority of Greenlandic communities to function independently with nearly no road networks apart from a few that link sheep farms in southern Greenland. Because of the difficulties involved in providing such essentials as power, water, and heating, these needs are serviced by a combination of national and local government entities.[REF] Therefore, any investment by non-allied nations in these utilities should be subject to Article X’s provisions because communities could effectively be held hostage if provision of these services were to be interrupted or maintenance were to be delayed.Finally, fisheries deserve attention with respect to critical investments in Greenland not only because they represent the primary national industry, but also because of the vital economic lifeline they provide for certain settlement economies.[REF] In addition, trends in ice distribution appear likely to herald an increase in fishing grounds off West Greenland that could spur economic growth in this sector.[REF] These economic opportunities could cement their outsized importance to the Greenlandic economy as consumer demand for seafood is expected to rise for decades;[REF] therefore, these benefits should be retained for local producers and fair partners.It should be noted that Denmark has already proven itself to be highly cooperative in this regard, having blocked the aforementioned attempt by a Chinese organization to purchase the abandoned Grønnedal naval base as well as another attempt by China to build new airports in Greenland.[REF]Permanence. One of the most important features of the updated 2026 agreement is that it addresses concern arising from the potential impact of Greenlandic independence by establishing that the agreement allowing the U.S. military presence, prohibiting non-NATO military bases, and establishing a mechanism for excluding malign investment by non-NATO governments will endure even if Greenland becomes independent. Specifically, the agreement provides that:In case Greenland exercises its right to self-determination to become independent, the Government of the Kingdom of Denmark and the Government of Greenland shall together ensure that the independent Greenlandic state will (i) agree to remain in NATO, including by applying to become a member if necessary, and (ii) affirmatively assume, as from the date of independence, all of the rights and obligations of the Kingdom of Denmark specified in this Agreement, including any implementation agreements or arrangements between the Parties, as well as the Defense Arrangements.[REF]ConclusionThe American, Danish, and Greenlandic peoples have a shared interest in a secure and sovereign Arctic where the shortest approaches to North America from Russia and China are secured and the rights of all Arctic states are respected. The September 2026 agreement protects the sovereign security and economic interests of Washington, Copenhagen, and Nuuk and helps to ensure transatlantic security cooperation through NATO in the Arctic for decades to come.[REF] This major diplomatic achievement expands U.S. defense areas in Greenland, prohibits non-NATO military presence, protects critical sectors of the Greenlandic economy that otherwise could have been exploited for dual-use purposes by adversarial governments, and permanently cements Greenland’s status and role in transatlantic security.Wilson Beaver is Senior Policy Advisor for Defense Budgeting and NATO Policy in the Douglas and Sarah Allison Center for National Security at The Heritage Foundation. Jordan Embree is a Senior Research Associate in the Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom at The Heritage Foundation.

    Sources indicate that president Donald Trump’s successful conclusion of the Greenland deal with the governments of Denmark and Greenland is a major achievement that will have positive security outcomes for the United States far into the foreseeable future. The agreement will also improve Danish and Greenlandic security, increase American military contributions to Arctic security, strengthen Greenland’s role in the transatlantic security architecture, and ensure that there is no risk of adversarial malign influence even if Greenland’s political status changes. From both the American and European perspectives, the agreement cements and expands the U.S. role in Arctic security, primarily through the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), and signals sustained American interest in transatlantic cooperation on Arctic security for many years to come.

    According to recent reports, critics have claimed that the deal is the same as before and that the new agreement does not provide anything the United States did not have before, which is demonstrably untrue.[REF] The 2026 agreement augments, updates, and improves the existing 1951 Defense Agreement: expanding U.S. military infrastructure on the island with new defense areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig that will host U.S. troops, creating a new mechanism for the prohibition of Russian or Chinese military bases in Greenland, and establishing a process for the governments in Copenhagen, Nuuk, and Washington to bar investment by non-allied states in critical sectors of the Greenlandic economy such as the mining sector, ports, and airports.[REF].

    The newly introduced agreement’s provisions would continue to apply even if Greenland were to become independent.

    The agreement details the core U.S. national security interests at stake and the rationale behind the push for an expanded agreement, “[r]ecognizing the security challenges in the Arctic and the High North posed by adversaries’ increased military activity and growing strategic interest in the region” and “[n]oting that the security situation in the Arctic is changing and that more efforts are needed to ensure security there in the future.”[REF].

    Sources indicate that the strategic rationale for American interest in securing Greenland from adversarial influence and maintaining a military presence is enduring, rational, and grounded in more than a century of U.S. strategic thinking.[REF] It is strongest when considered in the context of great-power competition and homeland defense, as the Arctic is the shortest and most likely path for strategic bombers or intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) heading toward the U.S. and Greenland in particular lies on the shortest and most likely path for these systems when they are fired from Russia.[REF] During the Cold War, both the United States and the Soviet Union operated submarines under the polar ice cap, tested weapons, and invested heavily in surveillance and early warning systems across the land, air, sea, and undersea domains because of the same geographic and strategic realities.

    Greenland commands the approaches to the North Atlantic and North America, forming the northwestern end of the Greenland–Iceland–U.K. (GIUK) Gap through which Russian ships and submarines entering the North Atlantic pass.[REF] It is crucial for the United States and its NATO allies to maintain awareness of Russian and Chinese submarines passing through this area, especially ballistic missile submarines equipped with nuclear weapons.

    It has been revealed that the airspace above Greenland is also critically key to defending the U.S. homeland, as U.S. military radars in Greenland contribute to the detection of any hostile ballistic missile movements toward North America.[REF] Because the Arctic is the shortest path between Russia and the United States and between China and the United States, Russian ICBMs, strategic bombers, and hypersonic and cruise missiles would most likely traverse the Arctic on course for the U.S. in the event of a war—a fact that led Washington to negotiate the 1951 Defense Agreement with Denmark early in the Cold War. North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD), a binational U.S.–Canada command, requires persistent Arctic and High North domain awareness to fulfill its core mission of defending the continent’s airspace.[REF] During the Cold War, the U.S. had an extended network of manned radar installations across the Arctic known as the Distant Early Warning Line (DEW Line), but it closed much of this network during the 1990s after the Cold War ended.[REF] The U.S. also operated a series of air and naval bases across Greenland that were likewise closed during the 1990s.

    Today, with the return of great-power competition with China and Russia, Washington has recognized the need to rebuild this Arctic infrastructure as an essential element of continental defense. Pituffik Space Base in Greenland is one of the central nodes in this architecture because its Upgraded Early Warning Radar is one of only a few U.S. or allied sensors providing ballistic missile warning and space surveillance coverage of the North Atlantic and polar approaches to North America.

    Sources indicate that the United States is increasing its engagement in the Arctic region in several ways, and the increased U.S. activity in Greenland is closely interconnected with other major national security projects being undertaken by the Trump Administration. For example, in view of the long-standing U.S. icebreaker shortage, Pituffik Space Base at the moment relies on a Canadian Coast Guard icebreaker for its annual resupply, given the longtime U.S. icebreaker shortage.[REF] The Icebreaker Collaboration Effort, or ICE Pact, seeks to remedy this shortage by building a much larger U.S. fleet of icebreakers in collaboration with Finland and Canada.[REF] The Trump Administration’s Golden Dome initiative to defend the North American continent from missile threats likewise has a major Arctic component and is mentioned in the Greenland agreement’s preamble as one of the shared interests of the three parties.[REF].

    Greenland is a self-governing part of the Kingdom of Denmark. It enjoys a significant degree of self-rule, but responsibility for defense and foreign policy remains primarily with the Danish government in Copenhagen.

    Industry observers note that greenland possesses substantial geological reserves of rare earth elements with 1.5 million tons of proven reserves and an estimated 36 million tons of total resources, putting it among the world’s top 10 countries in terms of geological assets. Greenland also possesses substantial uranium deposits as well as many other non–rare earth minerals with wide commercial applications.[REF] However, two principal difficulties—ice and regulation—will slow the pace of investment and development. The Greenland Ice Sheet extends across 656,000 square miles (roughly 80 percent of the country) and reaches thicknesses of more than 1.9 miles, making any significant extraction operation extremely complicated.[REF] With respect to regulation, Greenland banned uranium mining in 2021 and banned exploration of mineral deposits with even low levels (100 parts per million) of uranium, which caused a halt to a major rare earth mine because of colocation of minerals.[REF] If these difficulties are overcome, Western investment in Greenland could bring major secure upstream production of rare earth elements online.

    Industry observers note that the combination of a small population and a harsh and geographically isolating environment has caused the majority of Greenlandic communities to function independently with nearly no road networks apart from a few that link sheep farms in southern Greenland. Because of the difficulties involved in providing such essentials as power, water, and heating, these needs are serviced by a combination of national and local government entities.[REF] Therefore, any investment by non-allied nations in these utilities should be subject to Article X’s provisions because communities could effectively be held hostage if provision of these services were to be interrupted or maintenance were to be delayed.

    Finally, fisheries deserve attention with respect to critical investments in Greenland not only because they represent the primary national industry, but also because of the vital economic lifeline they provide for certain settlement economies.[REF] In addition, trends in ice distribution appear likely to herald an increase in fishing grounds off West Greenland that could spur economic growth in this sector.[REF] These economic opportunities could cement their outsized importance to the Greenlandic economy as consumer demand for seafood is expected to rise for decades;[REF] therefore, these benefits should be retained for local producers and fair partners.

    It should be noted that Denmark has already proven itself to be highly cooperative in this regard, having blocked the aforementioned attempt by a Chinese manufacturer to purchase the abandoned Grønnedal naval base as well as another attempt by China to build new airports in Greenland.[REF].

    Permanence. One of the most vital features of the updated 2026 agreement is that it addresses concern arising from the potential impact of Greenlandic independence by establishing that the agreement allowing the U.S. military presence, prohibiting non-NATO military bases, and establishing a mechanism for excluding malign investment by non-NATO governments will endure even if Greenland becomes independent. Specifically, the agreement provides that:.

    In case Greenland exercises its right to self-determination to become independent, the Government of the Kingdom of Denmark and the Government of Greenland shall together ensure that the independent Greenlandic state will (i) agree to remain in NATO, including by applying to become a member if necessary, and (ii) affirmatively assume, as from the date of independence, all of the rights and obligations of the Kingdom of Denmark specified in this Agreement, including any implementation agreements or arrangements between the Parties, as well as the Defense Arrangements.[REF].

    It has been revealed that the American, Danish, and Greenlandic peoples have a shared interest in a secure and sovereign Arctic where the shortest approaches to North America from Russia and China are secured and the rights of all Arctic states are respected. The September 2026 agreement protects the sovereign security and economic interests of Washington, Copenhagen, and Nuuk and helps to ensure transatlantic security cooperation through NATO in the Arctic for decades to come.[REF] This major diplomatic achievement expands U.S. defense areas in Greenland, prohibits non-NATO military presence, protects critical sectors of the Greenlandic economy that otherwise could have been exploited for dual-use purposes by adversarial governments, and permanently cements Greenland’s status and role in transatlantic security.

    Wilson Beaver is Senior Policy Advisor for Defense Budgeting and NATO Policy in the Douglas and Sarah Allison Center for National Security at The Heritage Foundation. Jordan Embree is a Senior Research Associate in the Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom at The Heritage Foundation.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, at matter in Viramontes (now Khaya) v. Cook County in the Supreme Court is the difference between fully automatic firearms such as the M-16 and semiautomatic rifles including the AR-15 platform. The following are a few excerpts from four amicus briefs establishing that the difference is fundamental.

    "But the M16 is capable of burst or fully automatic fire, meaning that a shooter can fire multiple rounds with a single function of the trigger. See Staples, 511 U.S. at 603. Fully automatic firearms 'were never in widespread civilian use' and have 'traditionally been banned' in the United States. Heller II, 670 F.3d at 1287 (Kavanaugh, J., dissenting). The AR-15, by contrast, is a semiautomatic firearm, meaning that it fires only one shot with each function of the trigger. See Cargill, 602 U.S. at 410–411, 416."  U.S. Br. 28.

    It has been revealed that "Semiautomatic rifles are in common use among law-abiding citizens for lawful purposes. 'The first commercially available semi-automatic rifles * * * entered the market between 1903 and 1906.' Heller II, 670 F.3d at 1287 (Kavanaugh, J., dissenting). Semiautomatic rifles 'have not traditionally been banned,' or even subjected to heavy regulation. Id. at 1269. Instead, they 'traditionally have been widely accepted as lawful possessions.' Staples v. United States, 511 U.S. 600, 612 (1994)." U.S. Br. 19–20.

    "A semiautomatic firearm fires one bullet for each trigger pull, while an automatic weapon (machine gun) fires continuously until the ammunition supply is exhausted, so long as the shooter presses and holds the trigger. See Staples v. United States, 511 U.S. 600, 602 n.1 (1994). 'The AR-15 is the civilian version of the military's M-16 rifle, and is…a semiautomatic weapon. The M-16, in contrast, is a selective fire rifle that allows the operator…to choose semiautomatic or automatic fire.' Id. at 603." Ballistic Experts Br. 6.

    Recent findings suggest that "Nor is an AR-15 'almost the same gun' as the military's M16 in the critical respect identified by federal law. Bevis, 85 F.4th at 1195. An ordinary AR-15 is semiautomatic: each trigger pull fires one round. A machinegun, by contrast, 'shoots, is designed to shoot, or can be readily restored to shoot, automatically more than one shot, without manual reloading, by a single function of the trigger.' 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b). That operational difference—not appearance or lineage—separates an ordinary semiautomatic AR-15 from an automatic machinegun." Cruz Br. 21.

    "In 1963, Colt submitted to the predecessor agency of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) two firearms for evaluation: a semiautomatic 'AR-15 Sports Version Rifle' and an 'AR-15 automatic rifle' (later renamed the M16). The agency found that modifications to the automatic version that made it into the Sports Version 'have changed the weapon in basic design to the extent that it is not a "firearm" in the machine gun category' as defined in the National Firearms Act." Second Amendment Law Center Br. 3.

    “It’s the economy, stupid.” That 1992 catchphrase by Bill Clinton advisor James Carville is being repeated in the aftermath of the Republican debacle last week. And it’s true that the economy can never be ignored. But “it’s the culture, stupid,” is a more apt refrain.

    It has been revealed that people, especially the young, voted nearly 10 socialists into the U.S. Congress, and socialists will now lead four of our largest and most important cities: Upcoming York, Los Angeles, Seattle, and our capital.

    Sources indicate that how did that happen in the Land of the Free, a country that used to have an in-built immunity to Marxism? Students for two or more generations have been acculturated to believe that Marxism is good and America is bad.

    Industry observers note that professors at these universities had to work assiduously. Americans’ resistance to Marxism used to be so strong that, according to urban legend, Soviet tyrant Josef Stalin was the first to coin the term “American exceptionalism” as he decried American imperviousness to the siren song of communism.

    Industry observers note that in June 1929, Jay Lovestone, leader of the Communist Party USA, visited Moscow to meet Stalin, and told him that the American worker was not interested in revolution. America’s lack of a feudal past, as well as other national character traits, made Americans inherently resistant. Stalin shot back that he was tired of this “heresy of American exceptionalism.”.

    >>> No, Mamdani, Socialism Does Not Increase Affordability.

    According to recent reports, that account, coming from Stalin’s biographers and popularized by the Atlantic, has been disputed, and Alexis de Tocqueville had already described the United States as “exceptional” in Democracy in America in 1835. But the story illustrates an vital point. America is exceptional in many important ways—like its unique adherence to Natural Right—but no longer when it comes to being immune to socialism.

    Voters last week elected six upcoming members of the Democratic Socialists of America to the House of Representatives: Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-NY); Claire Valdez (D-NY); Melat Kiros (D-CO); Donavan McKinney (D-MI); Chris Rabb (D-PA); and Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-CA).

    Industry observers note that this freshman class joins Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and Rashida Tlaib (D-MI), both first elected in 2018, and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT), who describes himself as a democratic socialist but is technically an independent.

    And of course, there is the new Mayor of Washington, D.C., Janeese Lewis George, who won 84% of the vote on Election Day, and Nithya Raman, the new mayor of Los Angeles, both proud socialists.

    The economy was the No. 1 reason voters gave for voting the way they did. Four in 10 voters named the economy, and 90% noted the cost of living was a crucial factor, according to The World Data.

    According to recent reports, color me skeptical. I agree more with economist Steve Moore, who noted on Fox News last Friday, after a stellar jobs report that beat expectations by a factor of 10,.

    I wish that would have come out a week ago, I mean, it could have changed things a lot. And by the way, I wrote a column the day after the election saying it wasn’t about ‘the economy, stupid,’ because the economy is pretty damn strong. I mean, you see it, everything that you all have been saying about what’s going on with construction, with manufacturing, with low unemployment rate, the fact there are more jobs than workers.

    Indeed, GDP is growing at an annualized rate of 3.4% in the last quarter. Private domestic demand is even stronger, rising almost 5%, the fastest in five years. The unemployment rate sits at 4.1%, and layoffs remain low.

    So, why are the voters so upset? It is true that young white males (a key Trump constituency in 2024) are having a tougher time, with the economy churning out more jobs that are geared to women, and because of discrimination against them due to diversity, equity, and inclusion targets, which continue despite Trump’s best efforts. These voters are facing real pressure points: housing, student debt, gas, groceries, etc.

    The Democrats were also disciplined in their messaging and had a great media ground game. The activist Van Jones explained on CNN that Democratic operatives had a coordinated social media campaign that involved tens of thousands of people acting through the “American Accountability Network,” a lefty consortium of content creators.

    >>> The Surprising New Guardians Of Liberty And What It Means For The Left.

    “The Republicans never figured out what we were doing,” remarked Jones, who, according to the writer Eitan Fischberger, claimed that this campaign generated 32.5 million daily hits on Instagram, 88.8 million on X and 185 million on Facebook, “driving the kitchen table affordability message and tying that to Democrats on a positive and Republicans on a negative.”.

    That voters then chose candidates with a socialist economic agenda that won’t address existing problems and has failed everywhere it’s been tried lies squarely on the capture by Marxists of the cultural institutions. Why do 60% of Democrats have a favorable view of socialism? They have been indoctrinated by the universities, the schools, the museums, the media, etc.

    Just ask conductor Andris Nelsons, who the Boston Symphony Orchestra fired as part of its ill-advised search for “relevance.” Nelsons brought increased ticket sales, but he was not aligned with the more “inclusive” direction the BSO is misguidedly taking.

    As Heather Mac Donald wrote on City Journal, “The main point of contention between the board and Nelsons … seems to have been the conductor’s allegedly inadequate enthusiasm for the race- and gender-based programming and hiring that became so dominant in the classical music world after the George Floyd riots.”.

    Any conservative who ignores all this, takes Carville to heart, looks at the election results and concludes that all the attention must be trained on the economy, to the exclusion of the oft-derided “culture wars,” will be making a massive mistake.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the midterm postmortem will continue for some time. Conservatives need careful data analysis from people who can interpret the numbers and understand politics, and politicians who can respond to public opinion with prudence and guiding rhetoric.But as The Daily Wire hosts noted, there is an even deeper problem that needs attention: no one has made a “robust argument for Americanism as an argument, a fully fleshed out argument.” What are the values that make America, America? What is the positive vision?America as a nation is defined by the organic intertwining of people, place, and principles. Each contributes something unique, and they reinforce one another to form a whole even greater than the sum of its parts.James Madison’s theory of separation of powers and checks and balances provides a helpful analogy. Each branch of government has particular responsibilities, but they are not strictly divided from one another. Instead, each branch holds pieces of the others. The president, for example, has the power to veto legislation, giving the executive branch a legislative function. With this dynamic, the three branches check each other to ensure that all act with fidelity and cohere as a single entity.>>> How To Win Back the Disillusioned American DreamThe same is true of the American nation of people, place, and principles.PeopleAmerica is a people sustained over generations by what Americans hold in common: language, history, traditions, and religion, to name a few. As John Jay wrote in Federalist 2:Providence has been pleased to give this one connected country to one united people—a people descended from the same ancestors, speaking the same language, professing the same religion, attached to the same principles of government, very similar in their manners and customs, and who, by their joint counsels, arms, and efforts, fighting side by side throughout a long and bloody war, have nobly established general liberty and independence.A shared culture binds Americans together and supports American principles. For example, speaking the same language allows neighbors to interact, thereby building goodwill and friendship. Communication also enables civic participation and deliberation, which are necessary for self-government.Religious institutions have historically played a major role in that deliberation. Churches are gathering places and seedbeds for community activity; they are the most notable civic associations. At the time of the Founding, 70–80% of American colonists attended services regularly, and the ideas of the Revolution, consistent with biblical principles, spread through sermons, pamphlets, and newspapers.Religion is not the only way a people sustain itself. As George Washington wrote in his Farewell Address, an individual can develop a moral framework independently, but “reason and experience both forbid us to expect that National morality can prevail in exclusion of religious principle.” The Founders and ancient philosophers alike argued that a republic cannot survive without a virtuous people, and religious belief and practice are indispensable for morality.PlaceHuman embodiment comes with an instinctive love of home. America’s physical wonders and gifts inspire awe and gratitude. A sense of reverence reigns over the places where many of our ancestors gave the last full measure of their devotion. And fondness builds in the communities where Americans practice civic rituals and raise posterity. These attachments are good and serious.Yet America as a place is even more: it has fostered American principles and formed the national character.From the outset, James Madison argued that America’s extended territory mitigates the problem of faction: groups adverse to the common good. America has numerous factions, which makes it harder for any single faction to gain a majority. Instead, people and representatives must work with one another and communicate to achieve their goals. That deliberative process slows things down and makes it more likely that justice will prevail.John Jay further observed that America was composed not of “detached and distant territories” but of “one connected, fertile, wide-spreading country” with a “succession of navigable waters” almost made “to bind it together.” The Founders’ response to America as a place was consistent with democratic principles and reinforced the sovereignty of the people.Through the Potomac River Project, which connected regions by roads and waterways, George Washington sought to bind the nation and the character of the American people. Thomas Jefferson led the repeal of primogeniture and entail laws in Virginia. The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 extended that vision to the frontier, and the taming of America’s heartland was given over to those who would steward the land, rather than left to be worked by the many and owned by a few aristocrats.The frontier spirit is part of the American heritage as a result. Americans are adventurous, informal, resilient, industrious, and somewhat gritty. Both the yeoman farmer and the entrepreneur animate the American moral imagination, as America’s physical resources, free institutions, and the human capacity for creativity unleashed profound prosperity.PrinciplesAmerica is the experiment in self-government, and self-government has a multi-layered meaning.Self-government at the institutional level means republican government, in which the people have a real say in the nation’s laws through mechanisms such as popular elections. As James Madison wrote, “no other form” of government “would be reconcilable with the genius of the people of America; with the fundamental principles of the Revolution; or with that honorable determination which animates every votary of freedom, to rest all our political experiments on the capacity of mankind for self-government.”As Madison suggests, self-government at the individual level underlies republican government. Because human beings have reason and conscience, they are responsible for their actions and can order reason above their passions and impulses.The maxim “all men are created equal” expressed in the Declaration of Independence recognizes the nature of human beings and situates mankind in an ordered universe. As John Adams wrote:[Equality] really means little more than that We are all of the same Species: made by the same God: possessed of Minds and Bodies alike in Essence: having all the same Reason, Passions, Affections and appetites. All Men are Men and not Beasts…. The blind are Men, and not Insects, the deaf are Men and not reptiles, the dumb are Men and not Trees. All these are Men and not Angells…America as a nation is dedicated to these principles, which define the American national character.As distinguished Washington and Founding scholar Dr. William B. Allen has written, Lincoln and others believed that regimes are guided by “a shared view of justice that makes a people a people. This was a very old idea, one expressed by Plato, and Aristotle, and Cicero, and Aquinas, and even Jefferson.”Shared understanding imposes limits on behavior and introduces the possibility of friendship, love, and goodwill. As a people, Americans have declared that “life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness” are inalienable rights, and that rights and duties are non-negotiable. Citizens can reasonably take for granted that neighbors will not use force or steal one another’s property, and those boundaries allow interaction and harmony.ConclusionArticulating a positive vision of the American nation helps identify policy solutions and cultural difficulties.Challenges to self-government include the growth of the administrative state and the erosion of deliberation by instant communication.>>> Freedom Isn’t Automatic—Each Generation Must Fight To Keep ItThis customizable and disembodied world erodes shared memories and experiences. Americans are less likely to gather for small-town parades and fireworks, as spending a solitary evening of Netflix and Uber Eats is more comfortable than eating a hot dog with a neighbor. For such reasons, preserving and defending the physical historic sites that transmit the American story and bring citizens together is even more urgent.Political and legal decisions have driven religion out of the public square, and churches have lost parishioners as they have diluted doctrine and required less of the human person.Immigration remains a concern as insular communities fail to assimilate into the American way of life. Explaining why others should assimilate requires educating the native-born population in the nation’s Founding principles, so its members can articulate why America is exceptional and worthy of loyalty.The nation’s Founding story teaches Americans who they are: a people committed to the principles of self-government, rights and duties, human equality, and the dictates of the natural order.These are just a few solutions that would reinforce people, place, and principles. Clarity about what constitutes the American nation guides policy prescriptions. Establishing that clarity is a necessary step in responding to the midterms.

    Providence has been pleased to give this one connected country to one united people—a people descended from the same ancestors, speaking the same language, professing the same religion, attached to the same principles of government, very similar in their manners and customs, and who, by their joint counsels, arms, and efforts, fighting side by side throughout a long and bloody war, have nobly established general liberty and independence.

    A shared culture binds Americans together and supports American principles. For example, speaking the same language allows neighbors to interact, thereby building goodwill and friendship. Communication also enables civic participation and deliberation, which are necessary for self-government.

    Religious institutions have historically played a major role in that deliberation. Churches are gathering places and seedbeds for community activity; they are the most key civic associations. At the time of the Founding, 70–80% of American colonists attended services regularly, and the ideas of the Revolution, consistent with biblical principles, spread through sermons, pamphlets, and newspapers.

    Religion is not the only way a people sustain itself. As George Washington wrote in his Farewell Address, an individual can develop a moral framework independently, but “reason and experience both forbid us to expect that National morality can prevail in exclusion of religious principle.” The Founders and ancient philosophers alike argued that a republic cannot survive without a virtuous people, and religious belief and practice are indispensable for morality.

    Place.

    Industry observers note that human embodiment comes with an instinctive love of home. America’s physical wonders and gifts inspire awe and gratitude. A sense of reverence reigns over the places where many of our ancestors gave the last full measure of their devotion. And fondness builds in the communities where Americans practice civic rituals and raise posterity. These attachments are good and serious.

    Yet America as a place is even more: it has fostered American principles and formed the national character.

    From the outset, James Madison argued that America’s extended territory mitigates the problem of faction: groups adverse to the common good. America has numerous factions, which makes it harder for any single faction to gain a majority. Instead, people and representatives must work with one another and communicate to achieve their goals. That deliberative process slows things down and makes it more likely that justice will prevail.

    John Jay further observed that America was composed not of “detached and distant territories” but of “one connected, fertile, wide-spreading country” with a “succession of navigable waters” almost made “to bind it together.” The Founders’ response to America as a place was consistent with democratic principles and reinforced the sovereignty of the people.

    Recent findings suggest that through the Potomac River Project, which connected regions by roads and waterways, George Washington sought to bind the nation and the character of the American people. Thomas Jefferson led the repeal of primogeniture and entail laws in Virginia. The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 extended that vision to the frontier, and the taming of America’s heartland was given over to those who would steward the land, rather than left to be worked by the many and owned by a few aristocrats.

    It has been revealed that the frontier spirit is part of the American heritage as a result. Americans are adventurous, informal, resilient, industrious, and somewhat gritty. Both the yeoman farmer and the entrepreneur animate the American moral imagination, as America’s physical resources, free institutions, and the human capacity for creativity unleashed profound prosperity.

    Principles.

    America is the experiment in self-government, and self-government has a multi-layered meaning.

    It has been revealed that self-government at the institutional level means republican government, in which the people have a real say in the nation’s laws through mechanisms such as popular elections. As James Madison wrote, “no other form” of government “would be reconcilable with the genius of the people of America; with the fundamental principles of the Revolution; or with that honorable determination which animates every votary of freedom, to rest all our political experiments on the capacity of mankind for self-government.”.

    As Madison suggests, self-government at the individual level underlies republican government. Because human beings have reason and conscience, they are responsible for their actions and can order reason above their passions and impulses.

    According to recent reports, the maxim “all men are created equal” expressed in the Declaration of Independence recognizes the nature of human beings and situates mankind in an ordered universe. As John Adams wrote:.

    It has been revealed that [Equality] really means little more than that We are all of the same Species: made by the same God: possessed of Minds and Bodies alike in Essence: having all the same Reason, Passions, Affections and appetites. All Men are Men and not Beasts…. The blind are Men, and not Insects, the deaf are Men and not reptiles, the dumb are Men and not Trees. All these are Men and not Angells….

    America as a nation is dedicated to these principles, which define the American national character.

    As distinguished Washington and Founding scholar Dr. William B. Allen has written, Lincoln and others believed that regimes are guided by “a shared view of justice that makes a people a people. This was a very old idea, one expressed by Plato, and Aristotle, and Cicero, and Aquinas, and even Jefferson.”.

    Shared understanding imposes limits on behavior and introduces the possibility of friendship, love, and goodwill. As a people, Americans have declared that “life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness” are inalienable rights, and that rights and duties are non-negotiable. Citizens can reasonably take for granted that neighbors will not use force or steal one another’s property, and those boundaries allow interaction and harmony.

    Conclusion.

    Articulating a positive vision of the American nation helps identify policy solutions and cultural difficulties.

    Challenges to self-government include the growth of the administrative state and the erosion of deliberation by instant communication.

    >>> Freedom Isn’t Automatic—Each Generation Must Fight To Keep It.

    In a recent development, this customizable and disembodied world erodes shared memories and experiences. Americans are less likely to gather for small-town parades and fireworks, as spending a solitary evening of Netflix and Uber Eats is more comfortable than eating a hot dog with a neighbor. For such reasons, preserving and defending the physical historic sites that transmit the American story and bring citizens together is even more urgent.

    Political and legal decisions have driven religion out of the public square, and churches have lost parishioners as they have diluted doctrine and required less of the human person.

    According to recent reports, immigration remains a concern as insular communities fail to assimilate into the American way of life. Explaining why others should assimilate requires educating the native-born population in the nation’s Founding principles, so its members can articulate why America is exceptional and worthy of loyalty.

    The nation’s Founding story teaches Americans who they are: a people committed to the principles of self-government, rights and duties, human equality, and the dictates of the natural order.

    It has been revealed that these are just a few solutions that would reinforce people, place, and principles. Clarity about what constitutes the American nation guides policy prescriptions. Establishing that clarity is a necessary step in responding to the midterms.

    • Cravath, Swaine & Moore’s associate salary scale was increased Tuesday, and it rivals the raises revealed in June at Milbank, according to coverage by Reuters.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 19, 2026, 11:56 am CST.

    Major U.S. law firms are giving associates raises and establishing a upcoming market rate ranging from $235,000 for first-year lawyers to $455,000 for senior associates, plus additional bonuses. (Image from Shutterstock).

    Recent findings suggest that major U.S. law firms are giving associates raises and establishing a latest market rate ranging from $235,000 for first-year lawyers to $455,000 for senior associates, plus additional bonuses.

    Cravath, Swaine & Moore’s associate salary scale was increased Tuesday, and it rivals the raises revealed in June at Milbank, according to coverage by Reuters.

    It has been revealed that milbank increased the associate salary range from $235,000 to $455,000. In July, it offered special bonuses between $6,000 and $25,000 for associates. Reuters is also reporting pay increases at Fried, Frank, Harris, Shriver & Jacobson and Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton.

    According to recent reports, cravath’s special bonuses—$11,000 to $40,000—based on class year, exceeded Milbank’s scale. Its year-end bonus scale starts at $15,000 and extends to $115,000, which is a continuation of what the firm and others offered in past years.

    No comments were given by Cravath.
