    #158863. The value of combining legal knowledge, technology, workflow design and project management in e-discovery

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2704 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abajournal ↗ Open Full Page

    The value of combining legal knowledge, technology, workflow design and project management in e-discovery

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ari Kaplan recently spoke with Chantelle Jalland, the associate director of advanced e-discovery and digital services for Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the United States at Ashurst Perkins Coie; and Satinder Soni, the managing director for the United Kingdom at Cimplifi.
    • Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Ashurst Perkins Coie.
    • Chantelle Jalland: I qualified as a lawyer in Australia almost 20 years ago, and when I moved to the U.K., I promptly moved into the world of e-discovery.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 20, 2026, 10:47 am CST.

    Ari Kaplan recently spoke with Chantelle Jalland, the associate director of advanced e-discovery and digital services for Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the United States at Ashurst Perkins Coie; and Satinder Soni, the managing director for the United Kingdom at Cimplifi.

    Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Ashurst Perkins Coie.

    Chantelle Jalland: I qualified as a lawyer in Australia almost 20 years ago, and when I moved to the U.K., I promptly moved into the world of e-discovery. At that stage, what attracted me to e-discovery was predictive coding, which meant the machine would learn from those decisions and reduce the need for humans in that really boring manual review phase. When we fast-forward to the release of gen AI, what was incredibly exciting for me was that you could use LLMs to code the documents from a prompt instead of that initial training round. In my current role, I feel incredibly fortunate to work with lawyers who want to use the latest technology to do things differently, so I don’t have to fight like I used to. My remit now at Ashurst Perkins Coie is much broader than e-discovery. I have a team that also builds custom AI solutions across transactional and advisory practice groups, so I very much appreciate the industry recognition moving toward this legal data intelligence.

    Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Cimplifi.

    Satinder Soni: I’ve been in the industry for over 20 years. My career started on the right side of the EDRM model, focusing on courtroom technology, transcription services and evidence presentation in court. E-discovery was just surfacing at that point. It really wasn’t a thing. I then moved into an e-discovery software company, which was acquired by several conglomerates. I then moved into a global risk consultancy, Control Risks, working with the investigations team on cyber breach investigations, digital forensics and e-discovery. I then moved to Ankura, which took a different approach to e-discovery, focusing more on analytics and subject-matter expertise in construction and turnaround restructuring, forensic accounting and white-collar crime investigations. Then I moved to Cimplifi, a U.S.-based company focused on e-discovery, investigations and contract analytics. They moved to the U.K. almost two years ago. Our U.S. clients had cross-border matters that needed U.K.-based expertise to be compliant with GDPR. We have grown our team here. We have a project management team with diverse professional skills, ranging from consultancies and accountancy firms to technology companies. It’s a great company to be in.

    Ari Kaplan: What’s making e-discovery more complex today, and how is that changing the way you approach each new matter at the outset?

    Chantelle Jalland: One of the biggest challenges is the size of new datasets. We had over 45 terabytes of data for a recent matter. I’ve handled some really large cases before, so this wasn’t the biggest, but given the facts of the case and the scope of the material concerns in the dispute, I expected the volume to be much smaller. It was a surprise, based on the facts, that it was that large, and it was simply the product of more data being created today. We also have platform switching. This morning, I was on a call with a colleague about a particular client matter, then received an email on the matter to an external party, then I had some internal Teams chat messages, and in one of those messages, they also shared a live document with status updates. That was all within a few minutes, so everything was moving so much faster, and there were four different sources of information on one particular matter or problem. If you think about that and expand it, if every single person is just adding this tiny bit of additional information, it’s going to lead to a data explosion. That’s also the biggest opportunity because the large matters are the ones that are interesting and exciting. They’ve got things that will go wrong or problems, and you want those differences to make it more interesting and something new to solve.

    Ari Kaplan: What e-discovery challenges do your clients most often ask you to solve?

    Satinder Soni: Everything has a different variable, and each e-discovery matter is a challenge because it is a reactive industry. Our clients come in quite hard and fast, and we have to take a step back to understand the data scoping. I have a separate challenge where they underestimate how much data there is, so you have to ease the shock of what it’s actually going to cost. But if you apply the right technology, phase it out, structure the workflow and talk them through it, the challenge then is pacing it, being realistic and providing timelines. The latest challenge really is applying AI into their workflows and driving the mindset shift they need to use a different type of analytics. They’ve just gotten used to CAL, and there is a bit of fatigue with it being more efficient and more cost-effective. We say it with every latest tool we bring in, and the challenge is always the mindset shift.

    Ari Kaplan: The Ashurst Perkins Coie Advanced Legal Solutions offering combines legal knowledge, technology, workflow design, project management and flexible resourcing. How does that combination enhance client service, and how do you define success before the work begins?

    Sources indicate that chantelle Jalland: There’s tremendous value in having multiple service offerings under one roof. We also have our risk advisory or consulting arm, which enables us to undertake deep data analytics tasks, and this gives us what we refer to internally as our triple threat. We have Advance, our fresh law arm, risk advisory and our core services team. Before the work begins, much of the success comes back to those foundational principles, and it builds on what Sati mentioned about managing expectations on timelines and being realistic. Historically, a partner will promise a client that we will deliver something in a certain amount of time for a certain cost, and that promise may not be realistic because the scope fundamentally changes or the expectation isn’t technically possible within the timeframe. They didn’t understand the basic principle that if you don’t understand the component, you can’t advise in that area, and that’s where we bring the right people into the conversation earlier. We have that open conversation and set small milestones or goals, so we’re meeting our client’s expectations along the way. And like everyone, I take great pride in an accurate cost estimate. But really, that data can expand at a different rate compared to a previous matter that you might have done an estimate on, or there’s a subset of data that’s got a processing error. There are so many things that can vary from what you might expect. As it shifts, it’s about having that conversation and letting everyone know it’s different from the original ask, and what I’ve found is clients appreciate that openness and willingness to have the conversation. You are advising, and there’s a lot more respect for the advice and the experience that can be offered in this area.

    Ari Kaplan: Where are clients rethinking their approach most often, understanding their data earlier, managing review, coordinating providers, or generally adjusting their litigation strategy?

    It has been revealed that satinder Soni: All of the above. E-discovery is a complex process. I’ve seen it where you’ve got your litigation strategy set, then you do the data scoping piece, and then you look at the early data and assess it. And when the review is happening, that’s when they realize we’re missing a custodian or this data source. Then the litigation strategy has to be readjusted. Then we go back to the data assessment. It can expand into other litigation support service lines, like asset tracing, or you need a forensic accountant. Chantelle put it really well. Communication is key. Understanding your stakeholders is part of that. Setting realistic timelines is part of that. It flits between the litigation strategy and understanding your data and that feedback loop.

    Ari Kaplan: What needs to happen earlier in a matter for a legal team, the e-discovery team and a service provider to work most effectively together?

    Industry observers note that chantelle Jalland: We tend to manage matters in-house with our legal team, but we also work with service providers on some matters. Sometimes a client has a preexisting relationship with a preferred provider, or we choose to engage a service provider due to their expertise. We recently had a matter involving historic offline databases that were in the format of a decommissioned product, so we needed to convert them for a current document review platform. It was more efficient to use an existing solution, rather than script something custom for that matter. What needs to happen to work effectively together is to get on a call early with all the right people. You can cut through so much with a phone call, making sure everyone is working toward the same blueprint from the outset.

    Ari Kaplan: When your team is engaged by a client under pressure, what distinguishes a trusted adviser from a provider that simply executes instructions?

    Satinder Soni: You should never be an order taker. Just because the client notes it, doesn’t mean it’s always the right thing. They come to us because we are experts in the field. They trust us to guide and support them through the process. Often, it goes wrong when the client calls, and everyone’s excited, and they dive right in, applying the same methodology from the previous project. Take a step back. Standard information to ask for at the beginning includes e-data, what has happened, the discovery objective, the goals they’re trying to achieve, and the timeline they’re working toward. Review data types, nonstandard files, foreign languages and whether the data is structured or unstructured. Really get into the details that will influence the e-discovery project and help it achieve its goals. We advise gathering as much information as possible in advance, so we can choose the right technology, manage timelines and predict accurate costs. In those instances, accurate cost prediction is also key. Our job as a trusted adviser is to say, “We can save costs if we do it this way.”.

    Ari Kaplan: Where is AI making the most meaningful difference in your work today, and where is its promise still a bit ahead of its practical value?

    Recent findings suggest that chantelle Jalland: AI has meaningfully changed my work. From a personal productivity perspective, AI call summaries make follow-up emails and meeting organization much easier. When I check a draft email, there are several small examples I use every day. On a larger scale, for high-impact matters, we have seen really effective use in due diligence, whether it’s legislative reviews for businesses or from an advisory perspective. The area where I see the most promise is large-scale document reviews. We are using AI for document review in a way that replaces CAL. So you filter down, you get a set of, say, 20,000 documents, and run it through. It is more effective than traditional manual review. It’s more effective than CAL. However, I see huge leaps ahead when it comes to document review. Most excitingly, I think, coming back to what Sati said earlier about working in a reactive industry, we are doing everything later. It’s actually about bringing those AI use cases further forward. Within a corporation, it’s about tracking themes, using the data more effectively, so you can identify the last 10 litigation matters or regulatory investigations that are actually costing you money, analyze that data, and then try to prevent future matters. That’s where it’s really exciting.

    Ari Kaplan: When would you choose not to use AI in a litigation support matter?

    Industry observers note that satinder Soni: We should all be using it in some way, shape or form. Traditionally, it was suggested that not all matters needed AI or analytics, either because it was cost-prohibitive, the dataset wasn’t compatible, or there wasn’t enough data to perform analysis. Recently, we’ve seen a shift toward using AI on small matters, such as DSARs. I have seen clients use AI on DSARs, and it seems effective. It frees up time for project managers to do more thoughtful work because DSARs don’t really go anywhere. They’re weaponized most of the time. So if they’re using it on investigation and litigation matters, their time is better spent. This is where AI can be used thoughtfully. There are still alternatives. CAL is being phased out, but it’s still there and still serves as a bridge to advising against linear review. But if people are not yet comfortable using AI, which hopefully they are, it’s in your everyday work now, so I just think, piece by piece, they’re trying it. I can’t think of any instance of not using AI.

    Ari Kaplan: As we leverage technology to perform more work, which human skills become increasingly valuable, and how do you develop them within your team?

    Industry observers note that chantelle Jalland: Communication is hugely important, so it’s something I’m focusing on from a recruitment perspective. We have to think about which skills can be taught and which are harder to teach. There’s analytical thinking. We need to make sure that the advisory stage isn’t so automated or process-driven that it’s replaced by AI. It’s about understanding that judgment is still needed and how to apply it. AI will be useful in many contexts, but how you use it will vary by use case. The risk is quite high if you don’t check the outputs, for example. It’s also about making sure people understand that risk. When it comes to training, it’s not a one-and-done. It’s continuous, and the same is true for communication. In a global law firm, different teams adopt different styles, and what works for one team doesn’t work for another. It’s about continuous learning without people feeling fatigued by constant learning.

    Ari Kaplan: What are the hallmarks of great client service in an AI-enabled environment?

    Satinder Soni: Great client service is all about communication, even when it’s bad news. Hopefully, it’s never bad news, but when it is, pick up the phone and have a conversation. We’ve gone crazy with short-form messaging, and what can be said in 10 emails can be said in a five-minute conversation. Then, with AI, be thoughtful about how we’re using it. Don’t fall into the trap of using AI for everything, and keep learning. There is a job you need to do: Put clients first, break down tasks, add structure to your work, and don’t just let AI take control.

    Ari Kaplan: How do you see e-discovery and legal tech evolving?

    Industry observers note that chantelle Jalland: I am very positive and optimistic about the future of e-discovery. There are many opportunities because, essentially, all the button-clicking will be gone soon, which is a great opportunity for people who work in e-discovery. You can apply a wide range of tools. It’s not just one technology. There are MCP connectors that you can use to adapt to certain platforms. So you are going to have so much more flexibility in the options. It does create more risk, potentially, if you’re not following a standard protocol, but what is exciting is that you can differentiate yourself in the market by specializing in solutions for certain use cases. Going back to first principles: understanding the problem, how you’re going to solve it, and considering all your options. It’s not going to be as linear. In the next five years, I would even say in the next year, we will be having a very different conversation about workflows in particular.

    Listen to the complete interview at Reinventing Professionals.

    Ari Kaplan regularly interviews leaders in the legal industry and in the broader professional services community to share perspective, highlight transformative change and introduce latest technology at his blog and on Apple Podcasts.

    Industry News: French Bill Risks Deepening Police Impunity

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (448 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The French Senate on November 20 approved a controversial bill that risks deepening impunity for use of lethal force by police.
    • The bill introduces a legal presumption of self-defense for law enforcement officers using firearms during the exercise of their duties, unless victims or their families can establish the use of lethal force was unlawful.
    • Because victims’ families lack access to key evidence to assess the legality of police-caused death, placing the burden of proof on them is likely to deepen impunity and seriously jeopardize pathways for accountability where lethal force was unlawful, unnecessary, or disproportionate.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The French Senate on November 20 approved a controversial bill that risks deepening impunity for use of lethal force by police.

    The bill introduces a legal presumption of self-defense for law enforcement officers using firearms during the exercise of their duties, unless victims or their families can establish the use of lethal force was unlawful.

    Because victims’ families lack access to key evidence to assess the legality of police-caused death, placing the burden of proof on them is likely to deepen impunity and seriously jeopardize pathways for accountability where lethal force was unlawful, unnecessary, or disproportionate. This is inconsistent with France’s human rights obligations with respect to protecting the right to life and use of force by law enforcement.

    The use of lethal force by police is a major concern in France. In 2023, a police officer fatally shot 17-year-old Nahel M., a racialized boy, during a traffic stop, triggering widespread scrutiny of police use of firearms.

    France’s national human rights body and the previous mandate holder of the independent ombudsperson as well as a United Nations rights expert raised serious rights concerns about the bill, while rights groups, activists, and legal professionals staged protests and petitioned parliament to stop the bill.

    The Senate’s vote followed approval of the bill by France’s National Assembly on July 7. Unless government officials or parliamentarians refer the bill for constitutional review, the president has 15 days to sign it into law.

    Since 2017, when lawmakers broadened the scope of permissible use of firearms by police well beyond international human rights standards requiring necessity and proportionality, numbers of fatal police vehicle stops in France have risen fivefold compared to before.

    In a recent development, A state cannot delegate its legal duty to investigate to those affected by lethal police force. This reversed burden of proof contravenes international human rights law, which requires states to thoroughly investigate every circumstance of lethal police force.

    Recent findings suggest that if the French authorities are serious about avoiding incidents of excessive use of lethal force, and rebuilding public confidence in policing, lawmakers should drop this bill. The government and parliament should instead focus legislative efforts on strengthening accountability and ensuring that police powers are subject to effective procedural safeguards to protect people from police abuse, discrimination, violence, and, increasingly, disproportionate use of firearms.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that azerbaijan’s parliament on November 18 approved sweeping amendments to legislation governing nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) that would expand government powers to suspend and dissolve independent groups, impose new registration requirements, and further restrict their operations. The following day, a court sentenced prominent rights defender Bashir Suleymanli to seven and a half years in prison, the latest in a series of harsh sentences against civil society activists prosecuted over foreign funding.

    It has been revealed that the proposed legislation would allow authorities, rather than courts, to suspend NGOs for up to a year for broadly defined violations, including failure to meet transparency and anti-money laundering requirements. It would also expand grounds for court-ordered dissolution to include activities deemed a threat to the “legally protected interests of the state and society”—vague standards open to abuse.

    Existing NGOs would have just 30 days after the law takes effect to revise their charters and apply for re-registration. The minimum capital to establish a nonprofit foundation, a type of nongovernmental organization, would increase tenfold, from 10,000 to 100,000 manats (approx. US$ 59,000). Together, these requirements would create additional barriers to establishing and maintaining independent civil society organizations in Azerbaijan.

    According to recent reports, human Rights Watch has documented how existing restrictions on registration and foreign funding have forced many independent groups to close or severely curtail their activities. The European Court of Human Rights has repeatedly found violations of freedom of association in cases involving Azerbaijani civil society organizations.

    Recent findings suggest that authorities took another strike at civil society on November 19 when the Baku Grave Crimes Court convicted Suleymanli, director of the Institute for Citizens’ Rights, of apparent politically motivated charges of money laundering and abuse of office. Arrested in March 2025, authorities prosecuted Suleymanli as part of a reopened investigation into foreign-funded NGO work.

    Courts have also handed down lengthy prison sentences to other activists prosecuted in connection with the same investigation, including eight years for Asaf Ahmadov and seven years and three months for Zamin Zaki (Zakiyev). Election monitor Anar Mammadli received a 13-year sentence in September following an unfair trial.

    Azerbaijani authorities should withdraw the proposed amendments, release Suleymanli and other civil society activists imprisoned for their legitimate work, and end the misuse of criminal law against independent groups. Azerbaijan’s international partners should press the government to uphold its obligations to protect freedom of association.

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, leaving the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, I can’t shake the disconnect between the reality of entire communities losing their homes to rising seas and some governments’ apathy and obstruction of the process.
    • According to recent reports, I am still in awe of Francis, a community leader from Solomon Islands who traveled to Antalya to share his story.
    • In a recent development, COP31’s inability to reach an overarching agreement leaves communities like Walande—and hundreds of other communities that have been forced to relocate—to face consequences of the climate crisis on their own.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, leaving the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, I can’t shake the disconnect between the reality of entire communities losing their homes to rising seas and some governments’ apathy and obstruction of the process. The conference ended without consensus on the proposed Antalya Pact—the overarching political agreement for the COP31 climate summit.

    According to recent reports, I am still in awe of Francis, a community leader from Solomon Islands who traveled to Antalya to share his story. “Walande… the birthplace written in my passport, no longer exists,” he told a hushed room. “It is submerged beneath the waves.” His words moved the high-level event’s moderator to tears.

    In a recent development, COP31’s inability to reach an overarching agreement leaves communities like Walande—and hundreds of other communities that have been forced to relocate—to face consequences of the climate crisis on their own. Despite coordinated calls from civil society, related outcome decisions do not include explicit discussion of displacement and planned relocation, and governments failed to increase funding to help frontline communities adapt. Nor was there recognition of the International Court of Justice’s landmark opinion affirming that governments have human rights obligations to address the climate crisis.

    Sources indicate that I leave Antalya holding both heartbreak and hope: the summit remains a vital space for global solidarity. Alongside partners in the Coalition on Dignified Climate Relocation, we brought frontline leaders, policymakers, and funders together to exchange lessons, and push for rights-respecting national policies and increased funding for communities forced to relocate. After watching our immersive documentary Solwata, several government officials and climate fund directors stepped up, committing to support finance and policies for relocating communities.

    Official negotiations fell woefully short, and the UN policy process failed to meet the moment in Antalya. But Marshall Islands, Bangladesh, Fiji, Nepal and other forward-thinking governments are proving that another path is possible. Dignified, rights-respecting solutions already exist—and they can be scaled up.

    Ethiopia, as host of COP32, should learn lessons from Australia and Türkiye’s failures, and center efforts to advance finance for adaptation and loss damage which are vital to protect the rights of climate displaced communities.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • I previously  wrote about Trump's new executive order seeking to deny birthright citizenship to various classes of children born on US soil, and noted the first legal challenges to it.
    • Judge Cooper rightly concludes that nearly all the various classes of children barred from birthright citizenship by the upcoming order are in fact protected by the reasoning of Barbara and other Supreme Court precedents, because they and their parents are clearly subject to US law, and required to obey it:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that yesterday, in the case of Nathan v. Trump, federal district Judge Christopher Cooper of the District of DC issued a ruling against Trump's latest executive order restricting birthright citizenship. The ruling is very similar to an earlier September decision by Judge Boardman of the District of Maryland. The one difference is that the class action injunction in Nathan covers a class that literally consists of all children illegally deprived of birthright citizenship under the new order, whereas the class in the Maryland case is slightly narrower.

    I previously  wrote about Trump's new executive order seeking to deny birthright citizenship to various classes of children born on US soil, and noted the first legal challenges to it. As I pointed out then, almost every part of the new order is at odds with the Supreme Court's recent ruling in Trump v. Barbara, which struck down Trump's executive order denying birthright citizenship to children of undocumented immigrants born in the United States, and those born to non-citizen parents here on temporary visas. The Fourteenth Amendment guarantees citizenship to all children "born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof." In Barbara, the Supreme Court majority made clear that "subject to the jurisdiction thereof" includes children of all persons who are subject to and required to obey US law.

    Judge Cooper rightly concludes that nearly all the various classes of children barred from birthright citizenship by the upcoming order are in fact protected by the reasoning of Barbara and other Supreme Court precedents, because they and their parents are clearly subject to US law, and required to obey it:.

    Sources indicate that earlier this year, the Supreme Court struck down President Trump's Executive Order 14160, which purported to deny citizenship to children born to parents temporarily or unlawfully present in the country. Those children, like "nearly all children born in the United States," the Court explained, are "citizens at birth" because they are born "subject to American law." Trump v. Barbara, 609 U.S. 719, 734–37, 740–41 (2026). Barbara reaffirmed that birthright citizenship extends to all but three narrow categories of children, each long understood to be beyond the Nation's governing authority at birth: children of foreign officials enjoying full diplomatic immunity, children of enemy forces in hostile occupation of U.S. territory, and children born aboard foreign public ships.

    Yet Barbara's ink had scarcely dried when the President issued a second executive order—Executive Order 14418, at issue here—directing federal agencies to withhold recognition of citizenship from additional categories of U.S.-born children with noncitizen parents. Among those now targeted are children whose parents work for foreign governments or international organizations but lack diplomatic immunity, children born through commercial surrogacy arrangements, and children with a parent suspected of membership in certain gangs or terrorist organizations. As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out latest exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws. The Court will therefore certify a class consisting of children who are or will be unlawfully denied citizenship under the Order. And it will preliminarily enjoin the Government from enforcing the Order against members of that class.

    As explained in my original August post on the latest executive order, that order covers four groups almost all of whose members are clearly subject to US law:.

    In a recent development, children of "alien enemies," defined as those where at least one of two non-citizen parents is a "designated Foreign Terrorist Organization under 8 U.S.C. 1189 or Specially Designated Global Terrorist, consistent with the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, 50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq., and Executive Order 13224 of September 23, 2001 (Blocking Property and Prohibiting Transactions With Persons Who Commit, Threaten to Commit, or Support Terrorism).".

    Children born to at least one non-citizen parent who is a "foreign government employee" or employed by an "international organization that possess[es] international-organization immunity.".

    Children where "either parent" has engaged in "birth tourist" transactions of various kinds (deliberately seeking to give birth in the US so the child would get birthright citizenship).

    Children "born in a territory or territorial waters of the United States where citizenship is not conferred by Federal statute." …[T]his only applies to children born in American Samoa, the one populated overseas US territory to whose residents Congress has not conferred citizenship by statute….

    As I explained more fully in my August post, all of the children in these four categories are obviously subject to US law, with the exception of those born to foreign diplomats who have diplomatic immunity. This latter group is already excluded from birthright citizenship. In that post, I also explained why the analogy between "alien enemies" (as defined in the order) and children of members of an invading army occupying US territory fails.

    In a recent development, judge Cooper's opinion analyzes all four categories thoroughly and effectively. He's particularly strong on the case of children of "alien enemies," a category which - he explains - the Trump order defines far more broadly than is justified by legal precedent, and which in any case does not include anyone not "subject to the jurisdiction" of the United States, because all such people are under US control and required to obey US law when on American soil. That differentiates them from the historically recognized exception for children of enemy troops in "hostile occupation" of US territory during a war. The US does not have effective jurisdiction over territory occupied by a hostile enemy army. But the last time any such thing occurred was during World War II, when the Japanese occupied a number of US island possessions in the Pacific.

    I noted some additional problems with Trump's "alien enemies" carveout in my August post about the second birthright citizenship order:.

    According to recent reports, finally, the [order is wrong about] children of "alien enemies," defined…. as members of various designated "terrorist" entities. If they enter the United States, they are subject to US law. That's why they can be prosecuted for any crimes they commit on US soil - including acts of terrorism!

    Members of these groups may be bad people. Some have committed horrendous crimes. But that is no reason to visit the sins of the parents upon the children. If a murderer or a rapist has a child born on US soil, the child is entitled to birthright citizenship, notwithstanding the reprehensible behavior of the parents. The same logic applies here.

    It is also worth noting that the "foreign terrorist organization" (FTO) designation has been slapped onto various groups that are not actually terrorists in the ordinary meaning of the word, most notably groups engaged in smuggling illegal drugs.

    Trump may be trying to use the "alien enemy" designation here to analogize these children to children of members of an invading army, born  at a time and place where the invaders have seized control of US territory, thereby preventing the exercise of US "jurisdiction." Trump v. Barbara reaffirms the longstanding view that such children are excluded from birthright citizenship, because born in an area where US jurisdiction does not (at the time) meaningfully apply.

    But FTOs have not, in fact, "invaded" or occupied any part of the United States. Thus, US jurisdiction still applies. Therefore, children of members these organizations are not analogous to children born to members of an occupying foreign army. No part of the United States has actually been invaded and occupied since the Japanese seized various US territories in the Pacific during World War II.

    In my article, "Immigration is Not Invasion….," I explain in much more detail why the activities of drug dealers do not qualify as an "invasion," why an FTO designation cannot change that reality, and why courts should not defer to the president's claims that an "invasion" has occurred.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 20, 2026, 11:10 am CST.

    Industry observers note that consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both mentioned they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that new candidates emerged after Weil, Gotshal & Manges’ collapse. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    The fall of Weil, Gotshal & Manges is pushing law firm leaders to rethink strategy, and many are looking to find merger partners.

    According to a Thursday story by Law.com, consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both mentioned they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that fresh candidates emerged after Weil Gotshal’s collapse.

    “Many conversations were put on hold earlier this year to watch where the economy was going, how AI was going to effect the transformation of law firms,” Grossman told Law.com, adding that interest in mergers “was picking up over the summer, but now the pace is getting faster.”.

    “A large and growing group of firms want considerably larger balance sheets, greater long-term stability, more money to invest in talent and technology, and other advantages that come with scale,” Zimmermann added.

    Lisa Smith of Fairfax Associates offered a slightly different read, telling Law.com that merger demand was already strong in 2026, and Weil Gotshal mainly added urgency for firms that were already considering deals.

    “The lesson of Weil is that for firms that are looking to grow and looking to grow via merger or particularly for those starting to see some cracks in the firm, it’s notable to go to the merger market while you’re still in a strong position,” Smith noted to Law.com.

    Smith suggested that firms should approach the merger market from a position of strength. Firms that wait until trouble sets in risk becoming what advisers call a “falling knife,” an unstable partner few want to take on.

    Industry observers note that “We’ve seen a number of occasions over the last few years where a firm needed to merge with a ‘white knight’ and can only get that when the firm is strong enough to be a desirable acquisition,” Smith noted. “For firms that start to see signs that the future is going to be more challenging, it’s key to look at their options early.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that (London) – Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government has systematically weakened institutions established to protect human rights and democratic freedoms, Human Rights Watch noted in a report released today. Indians have increasingly taken to the streets to protest government repression, corruption, and a deeply flawed revision of voter lists.

    The 95-page report, “‘So What’s This Democracy We’re Talking About?’: Modi’s Authoritarian Playbook in India,” finds that the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government is undermining parliamentary procedures, suppressing the political opposition, and weaponizing federal investigative agencies for political ends. Human Rights Watch found that the government is also weakening constitutional and statutory bodies, such as the Election Commission, Central Information Commission, the anti-corruption ombudsman, and human rights commissions, and interfering in the judicial branch.

    Modi’s Authoritarian Playbook in India.

    Download the full report in English.

    Industry observers note that “Over the past decade, the Modi government has been hollowing out India’s independent institutions that are critical to checking executive power and protecting civil liberties,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The government has eroded the rule of law and promoted Hindu majoritarianism, rolling back human rights protections, undermining the rights of marginalized communities, and deepening India’s authoritarian slide.”.

    Human Rights Watch interviewed over 40 lawyers, journalists, activists, researchers, academics, current and former judges, and former government officials between January 2025 and September 2026.

    The Modi administration has frequently disregarded parliamentary oversight mechanisms to impose its political agenda. In December 2023, the government adopted a law that entrenched executive control over the appointment of election commissioners and granted them sweeping legal immunity for actions, decisions, or statements made while carrying out their official duties. The law was passed even as opposition members were suspended in unprecedented numbers from both houses for the entire session of the parliament, 100 from Lok Sabha (the House of the People or lower house) and 46 from Rajya Sabha (the Council of States or upper house).

    The BJP did not have a majority in the Rajya Sabha from 2014 to 2024. While all bills must be approved by both houses to become law, some regulating financial matters can be introduced in the Lok Sabha as “money bills,” which do not require Rajya Sabha approval. The Modi administration aggressively used money bills to push through laws with serious consequences for fundamental rights that would not qualify as money bills.

    Recent findings suggest that in 2019, the government used this approach to amend the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, significantly expanding the authority of the Enforcement Directorate, the federal enforcement agency it has used to improperly target political opponents, activists, and critics. The expansion of Enforcement Directorate powers would not appear to fall within the parameters set out for a money bill.

    The Election Commission has repeatedly failed to hold Modi and senior BJP leaders to account despite apparent violations of the election code of conduct by use of hate speech. The commission has also failed to credibly investigate allegations by voters, activists, academics, and political parties of manipulation of registered voter lists, suppression of polling data, irregularities in counting votes, or interfering with voting machines.

    In a recent development, the commission is at the moment facing a massive crisis of credibility amid concerns over its ability to function independent of the executive. A Special Intensive Revision, purportedly to delete dead, duplicate, or ineligible voters, has arbitrarily removed over 130 million names from electoral rolls since June 2025, sparking nationwide protests in October 2026.

    The administration has used federal agencies to pressure members of rival parties to defect to the BJP. After amending the law against money laundering, official data shows that the Enforcement Directorate filed cases against 193 politicians between April 2015 and February 2025, most of whom were government opponents. This was more than a 600 percent jump from the 26 politicians investigated in the decade preceding the Modi administration. Such investigations are promptly stalled, or charges are dropped if the accused switches loyalties, leading opposition parties to call the BJP a “washing machine.”.

    Sources indicate that the Modi government has since 2014 increasingly used federal investigation agencies to target domestic and international rights groups, human rights lawyers, activists, and media organizations under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act and other laws dealing with financial irregularities. It has used the abusive counterterrorism law, the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), to wrongfully jail human rights activists, journalists, students, peaceful protesters, academics, and critics, sometimes for years without trial.

    It has been revealed that india’s courts have also failed to uphold fundamental freedoms. In 2022, the Supreme Court endorsed and expanded the authority of enforcement agencies for arrest and search and seizure under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act. Legal scholars criticized the verdict as gutting rights to life and liberty.

    The Supreme Court is currently hearing petitions regarding the legitimacy of the electoral roll revision process. In May 2026, even after millions of names had been eliminated from voter lists, the court ruled that the data did not indicate “systemic disenfranchisement.” In April, after 9 million names—12 percent of the electorate—in West Bengal state had been removed, the court effectively remarked it was acceptable for them not to vote at that time so long as they would be added back to the rolls. Shortly afterward, the BJP won control of the state for the first time. By November, the Election Commission, after protests, started reversing some of the decisions that had led to the arbitrary removal of names.

    According to recent reports, the Modi administration’s actions over the past decade are not isolated institutional failures but mutually reinforcing elements of an authoritarian playbook, Human Rights Watch said. A weakened opposition has fewer means to resist laws that entrench executive control. Institutions led by political appointees, such as the federal and state human rights commissions, have not adequately responded to efforts to prevent the silencing of civil society. When courts fail to provide timely and effective remedies, these abuses go unchecked.

    India’s allies should publicly and privately raise concerns about ongoing abuses and the deterioration of democratic institutions, including during high-level engagements and interactions, at the United Nations Human Rights Council, and in negotiations for bilateral trade and security agreements.

    It has been revealed that “Checking India’s democratic decline means ending the use of state institutions as weapons against government critics and rebuilding them as safeguards for everyone’s rights,” Pearson stated. “India’s allies should press the Modi government to end its assault on independent institutions and restore checks on executive power.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Brussels, November 24, 2026) – Croatian authorities routinely engage in pushbacks at the border, including of unaccompanied children and families with young children, despite European Union efforts to end the practice, Human Rights Watch remarked in a report released today.

    It has been revealed that the 43-page report, “Doing Europe’s Dirty Work: Ongoing Violent Pushbacks of Migrants from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina,” finds that Croatian authorities routinely engage in pushbacks, often violently. An EU-funded Croatian border monitoring program has had little impact on Croatian police pushbacks. Instead, the EU has increased funding to Croatia for border management without addressing the abuse at the border.

    Ongoing Violent Pushbacks of Migrants from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

    Download the full report in English.

    Download the Summary & Recommendations in Bosnian.

    Download the Summary & Recommendations in Croatian.

    Annex: Unofficial Translation of the Croatia Ministry of Interior's Response to Human Rights Watch.

    Croatia Ministry of the Interior's Response to Human Rights Watch (Original Email in Croatian).

    Recent findings suggest that “Violent pushbacks by Croatian police are a continuing issue, affecting children as well as adults, and the EU-funded systems set up to curb them aren’t working,” stated Michael Garcia Bochenek, senior children’s rights counsel at Human Rights Watch. “The EU needs to act to ensure that Croatia respects EU law and protects the rights of those at its borders.”.

    Human Rights Watch interviewed more than 80 people, including seven unaccompanied children, four children travelling with family members, and six parents travelling with their children, and also interviewed 15 aid workers and others who offer information and other support to asylum seekers and migrants.

    Industry observers note that people interviewed said that Croatian police beat or kicked them, took all their money, and confiscated or destroyed their phones. In some cases, people said, the border police seized their documents, took their shoes, or even forced them to strip to their underwear before pushing them back across the border.

    According to recent reports, “We told them that we are a family, but [the Croatian police] still took my husband away in one van and me and my daughters in another,” noted a woman from Ghana. “We were separated for two days from my husband. They pushed me and my daughters to Bosnia through the woods. No phone, no food, no water. We were walking all day. We were lost and scared for many hours.”.

    Croatian authorities demonstrate official tolerance for unlawful police pushbacks through inadequate oversight, ineffective investigations and a lack of meaningful accountability, and repeated minimization—and often outright denial—of these practices, Human Rights Watch found. The government has not prosecuted any police officers for taking part in pushbacks, even in cases in which people suffered serious injuries or extreme forms of humiliation. Seven officers received disciplinary sanctions for mistreatment of migrants between 2020 and 2025, the Croatian Interior Ministry told Human Rights Watch.

    The only accommodation option in Bosnia and Herzegovina for most people pushed back from Croatia, including unaccompanied children and families with children, is the Lipa Migrant Reception Centre, 25 kilometres from Bihać, the nearest city. The center has experienced water shortages and power outages and has no local bus service. Healthcare services are limited, and the center provides no education for children.

    To its credit, the Croatian government strengthened the authority of a border monitoring mechanism established in 2021 with EU funding to prevent and address pushbacks and other abuses at the border.

    But the program has had little impact on Croatian police pushbacks, which remain common, Human Rights Watch remarked.

    European Union institutions have tools for direct oversight and enforcement of Croatia’s adherence to human rights, refugee, and EU norms, including the prohibition of collective expulsion—removing people without an individualized examination of their circumstances—as well as the best interests of the child, the right to seek asylum, and the prohibition of torture and other ill-treatment. But it has not used its authority to end the pushbacks. Instead, the EU has promoted and funded increased external border control by Croatia at the expense of people’s rights and protection needs.

    The European Commission can open infringement proceedings against an EU member state that fails to implement EU law. The European Parliament can examine violations of EU law by member states. Neither has taken place in respect of Croatia’s border abuses.

    According to recent reports, the European Rule of Law Mechanism allows an annual dialogue between the European Commission and member states. Recent rule of law reports have not examined the weaknesses of Croatia’s border monitoring mechanism, nor have they addressed pushbacks more directly.

    Croatian authorities should immediately end pushbacks at its borders, provide opportunities to seek asylum, and ensure that the new border monitoring mechanism is a robust and independent safeguard against pushbacks and other official abuse, Human Rights Watch stated. The European Commission should withhold border control funding until Croatia investigates and ends pushbacks and other mistreatment.

    Authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina should move families with children and unaccompanied children to facilities that are appropriate for their needs. The authorities should also ensure that all temporary reception centers, including for adults, are accessible by public transit and to shops, schools, hospitals, and other essential services.

    The EU and its member states should also create pathways for safe, orderly, and regular migration, Human Rights Watch said.

    “The EU needs to act to end the violent and abusive pushbacks at its borders and to hold Croatia to account for persistent and flagrant violations of EU law and international norms,” Bochenek said.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, (Geneva, November 24, 2026) – New use, production, and acquisition of antipersonnel landmines contributed to killing or injuring at least 6,929 people in 2025, which is the highest annual total since 2020, Human Rights Watch said today with the release of the “Landmine Monitor 2026” by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, (Geneva, November 24, 2026) – New use, production, and acquisition of antipersonnel landmines contributed to killing or injuring at least 6,929 people in 2025, which is the highest annual total since 2020, Human Rights Watch said today with the release of the “Landmine Monitor 2026” by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines. Human Rights Watch is a founding member of the campaign and contributed to the report.

    In a recent development, the 200-page report examines global compliance with the 1997 Mine Ban Treaty and the challenges facing the treaty nearly three decades after its adoption. The treaty comprehensively bans antipersonnel mines and commits countries to eliminate stockpiled weapons, clear contaminated land, and assist mine victims and affected communities.

    “At a time when civilian casualties are rising and fresh technologies make mines easier to deploy, supporting the Mine Ban Treaty is more crucial than ever,” mentioned Verity Coyle, deputy crisis, conflict and arms director at Human Rights Watch. “All countries should join the treaty, and members should fully uphold its obligations.”.

    Antipersonnel mines continue to kill and maim civilians long after fighting moves elsewhere. Whether they are placed by soldiers on the ground or delivered remotely by weapons systems and drones, the mines contaminate land, roads, and communities for years. Their presence can prevent displaced families from returning home, obstruct humanitarian operations, and undermine efforts to rebuild livelihoods and food production.

    According to recent reports, A total of 162 countries are now bound by the Mine Ban Treaty. Three countries joined during the reporting period: Lebanon, Marshall Islands, and Tonga. Five other countries withdrew from the treaty in 2025 and 2026: Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland.

    Ukraine revealed on July 18, 2025, that it would “suspend the operation” of the treaty while engaged in armed conflict with Russia, citing Russia’s extensive use of landmines. Suspensions, however, are unlawful under the treaty, notably during armed conflict, and Ukraine remains fully bound by all the treaty’s obligations. During the reporting period, Ukraine has acquired, produced, and used newly assembled antipersonnel mines, including types that are delivered by drone, in violation of the treaty.

    In addition to Ukraine’s use of antipersonnel mines, states not party to the treaty used them, including Iran, Myanmar, North Korea, and Russia.

    In a recent development, antipersonnel mines were increasingly used in border conflicts, involving Cambodia and Thailand, Bangladesh and Myanmar, and in Thailand along the borders with Myanmar and Malaysia. Non-state armed groups also used antipersonnel mines, in many cases improvised, in Colombia, India, Myanmar, Pakistan, Sudan, and in locations in Western and Central Africa, including in the Chad Basin, Burkina Faso, and Mali.

    Sources indicate that the Landmine Monitor reported that 15 states not party to the treaty either currently produce antipersonnel mines or maintain the option to produce them in the future. Of these, India, Myanmar, Poland, Russia, and South Korea appear to be actively producing or developing antipersonnel mines. Finland, Latvia, and Lithuania—all of which withdrew from the treaty in 2025—have indicated their intent to develop or acquire antipersonnel mines. Non-state armed groups have produced improvised mines that explode due to the presence, proximity, or contact of a person in Colombia, India, Africa’s Sahel region, and sporadically in Thailand.

    In 2025, casualties from antipersonnel landmines and explosive remnants of war occurred in at least 54 countries and areas. Of these, 39 are party to the Mine Ban Treaty. Myanmar, which is not a party, recorded the highest number of annual casualties (1,891) for the third consecutive year, and Syria recorded 1,602 casualties. Civilians made up at least 84 percent (5,078) of all recorded casualties, while children accounted for 50 percent (1,690) of civilian casualties where the age group was known.

    In a recent development, even as renewed mine use is contaminating fresh territory, progress remains possible. Croatia declared completion of its mine clearance obligations in March 2026, following Oman in 2025. Since the Mine Ban Treaty entered into force in 1999, 32 states parties have successfully cleared all known antipersonnel mine contamination from their territory.

    The near elimination of government stockpiles remains one of the treaty’s greatest achievements. Of the 162 states parties, 157 report that they do not possess stockpiled antipersonnel mines. Ninety-four countries have finished destroying their stocks, a total of more than 55 million mines. As during previous reporting periods, Greece and Ukraine continue to possess stockpiles of antipersonnel mines, in violation of article 4 of the treaty.

    “The world should be moving closer to ending the suffering caused by antipersonnel mines, not witnessing a resurgence in their use,” Coyle said. “Governments should be seeking global adoption of the ban treaty and reinforcing compliance, not stepping away from one of the world’s most successful humanitarian disarmament treaties.”.

    Industry observers note that the “Landmine Monitor 2026” is the 28th annual publication by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines, the global coalition of nongovernmental organizations that received the 1997 Nobel Peace Prize. Human Rights Watch co-founded the campaign in 1992 and contributes to its Landmine Monitor reporting initiative.

    2026 Year in Review: When AI dominated the room

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1047 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that I’ve been writing this column for nearly nine years, and over the past year, I’ve seen legal professionals adapt to upcoming technology faster than ever before.
    • At record pace, established legal technology companies have embedded AI into their products, rolled out AI-enabled features, and connected consumer-grade AI to their platforms using model context protocol connectors.
    • It was a year of rapid change, making it challenging for lawyers to keep up.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that I’ve been writing this column for nearly nine years, and over the past year, I’ve seen legal professionals adapt to upcoming technology faster than ever before. At the same time, technology has advanced exponentially, with artificial intelligence changing how information is obtained and how work gets done.

    At record pace, established legal technology companies have embedded AI into their products, rolled out AI-enabled features, and connected consumer-grade AI to their platforms using model context protocol connectors. Meanwhile, AI startups proliferated across the legal technology landscape, with some disappearing overnight, while others were snapped up and acquired less than a year after launch.

    It was a year of rapid change, making it challenging for lawyers to keep up. From tracking updated software features and emerging AI-powered technologies to learning how to use AI ethically, lawyers had a lot on their plates. That’s where my 2026 columns came in. Each one offered a summary of the latest legal technology news or provided roadmaps for legal software adoption in law firms.

    In a recent development, trusts and estates lawyers rely on drafting software to create complex planning documents and manage related estate work. These tools include features like guided interviews, automated forms and shared client information that support document creation and reduce drafting errors. Some software also helps lawyers customize plans and handle tasks such as trust funding and estate administration. Understanding how the options differ can assist lawyers in choosing the software that fits their trusts and estates practice’s workflows.

    AI systems reflect the assumptions and perspectives of the people who develop them, as well as the data used to train them. Those assumptions can shape AI outputs and reinforce bias, especially when women and other underrepresented groups have little input into how systems are designed. Drawing on the Women + AI Summit, including more perspectives when developing AI matters; it can impact the questions considered, improve outcomes, and determine how these systems affect consumers and the public at large.

    Industry observers note that at Legalweek 2026, agentic AI and the competition to become law firms’ central AI platform were recurring themes. There were also plenty of updates from legal technology providers, from platforms that connected research, drafting and firm data to specialized tools for e-discovery, litigation, legal research and skills training. The conference announcements highlight how companies are building both integrated ecosystems and focused applications that help lawyers incorporate upcoming AI-driven workflows into their firms.

    In a recent development, drawing on findings from the 8am 2026 Legal Industry Report, this column examines how the profession is responding to rapid AI adoption, access-to-justice hurdles and concerns about the rule of law. The report shows that individual AI use has grown faster than the implementation of firm policies and training, even as survey respondents see technology as one way of bridging the access-to-justice moat. Also notable was that lawyers were most concerned about the rule of law and its continued degradation.

    The growing number of court filings with fabricated or inaccurate case citations has led to a fresh category of tools designed to check AI-generated legal documents. Citation checkers can help identify false citations, misquoted language and inaccurate descriptions of case holdings. There are citation-checking tools built into drafting platforms in addition to those found in stand-alone applications, with a focus on their capabilities and costs. Before investing in a new tool, consider whether the time saved through AI research, drafting and citation checking justifies the expense or whether traditional research and drafting may ultimately be more cost-effective.

    It has been revealed that as AI takes on routine work traditionally assigned to junior lawyers, it may also reduce opportunities to develop practical legal skills. Training platforms can allow law students and early-career lawyers to build experience through courtroom simulations, interactive exercises and AI- or VR-based practice. These tools allow customers to rehearse tasks, such as deposition questioning, negotiation and courtroom advocacy, with some offering immediate performance feedback. Using these simulation-based learning platforms, recent law school graduates are better able to bridge the experiential gap and ensure that they have the building blocks needed to thrive in the AI era.

    Industry observers note that partnerships and integrations dominated the news at ILTACON 2026, as legal technology companies worked to connect their AI tools with legal data, software and workflows. In addition to those developments, there were new products that streamlined litigation, legal writing and law firm pricing. The conference takeaway was that legal AI is moving beyond stand-alone tools toward connected systems, for better or for worse.

    Sources indicate that litigation teams often work with large, complex collections of digital evidence, which can be difficult to organize and analyze using traditional methods. AI-powered fact analysis tools can assist with the review of case materials by identifying people, events and inconsistencies and by creating timelines that link to supporting documents. These tools can help litigators analyze and understand the evidence and collaborate more efficiently with their teams.

    Sources indicate that as fresh AI-powered platforms enter the market, solo and small-firm lawyers now have more affordable options for legal research. There are some tools priced at $100 or less per month that lawyers can use to rapidly and easily search caselaw and statutes. Some also offer case analysis and citation-checking tools to confirm subsequent case treatment. These platforms provide smaller practices with more options, but lawyers should still weigh the cost and accuracy rates against existing research tools, along with the time required to verify AI-generated results.

    Industry observers note that nicole Black is a Rochester, New York-based attorney, author and journalist. She is the principal legal insight strategist at 8am, parent company of LawPay, MyCase, CasePeer and DocketWise. She is the nationally recognized author of Cloud Computing for Lawyers and is a co-author of Social Media for Lawyers: The Next Frontier, both published by the American Bar Association. She writes regular columns for ABAJournal.com and Above the Law, has authored hundreds of articles for other publications, and she regularly speaks at conferences regarding the intersection of law and emerging technologies.     📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Brussels) – Companies that receive complaints of forced labor in their operations or supply chains should make sure affected workers have access to full and effective remedies, Human Rights Watch and a group of civil society organizations and trade unions mentioned in a report released today.

    In the White Paper on Remediation of Forced Labour in the Private Economy, the organizations set out what appropriate and effective remedies look like for workers, and the concrete steps companies should take to deliver it.

    “Forced labor does not end when a product is pulled from the shelves but only when workers who were trapped by debt, deceived, or threatened get their wages, documents, and dignity back,” mentioned Hélène de Rengervé, senior advocate at Human Rights Watch. “Companies should remedy labor abuses in their supply chains and engage with workers from the start to define appropriate solutions.”.

    It has been revealed that the groups propose concrete steps for companies to prepare, deliver and assess their remediation obligations. The report comes as the European Union prepares to enforce its Forced Labour Regulation, which will ban products made with forced labor from the EU market across all sectors and stages of production beginning on December 14, 2027. Under the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, companies in its scope will also have a legal duty to remedy harm they cause, completely or in part.

    In a recent development, an estimated 17.3 million people were in situations of forced labor in the private economy in 2022, according to global estimates by the International Labour Organization (ILO), Walk Free, and the International Organization for Migration. The number of victims increased by 8 percent between 2016 and 2021. The ILO estimates that forced labor in the private economy generates US$63.9 billion in illegal profits every year.

    In a recent development, academics and experts found that forced labor is rarely only the result of a few bad actors, but is rooted in poverty, discrimination, weak labor protections, and restrictive migration regimes. Migrant workers face heightened risks, including recruitment fees that lead to debt bondage, deceptive recruitment practices, and visas tied to a single employer. Fear of deportation and retaliation often keeps victims from seeking redress.

    The civil society groups said that companies should put in place remediation measures that restore as much as possible the situation for workers if the abuse had not occurred. This would require the cessation of the abuse, restitution, rehabilitation, compensation, apologies, and guarantees of non-repetition. Companies should also ensure that workers and their representatives can identify abuses through grievance mechanisms they trust, define remedies, and assess whether they have been delivered to their satisfaction, the groups said. At all times, affected workers should be protected from retaliation.

    Companies should treat remediation as part of their human rights due diligence, not as a one-off response to a scandal, the groups mentioned. Their responsibility should reflect their involvement in failing to prevent or meaningfully address the harm. Companies should not “cut and run” from suppliers when and where labor abuses, including forced labor, is found, as this can leave workers worse off. Instead, the groups said, companies should fairly agree on how to address and share remediation costs.

    To prevent forced labor from occurring and recurring, companies should examine structural causes such as poverty, discrimination and impairments to freedom of association but also how their own purchasing practices may drive it. They should pay to cover the cost of decent working conditions and living wages. The groups point to worker-driven models, such as the Fair Food Program in US agriculture and the Dindigul Agreement in India’s textile sector, as evidence of good practices.

    It has been revealed that the EU and its member states should ensure that the competent authorities empowered to enforce the Forced Labour Regulation assess whether effective remediation has actually delivered for workers, including through workers’ own accounts and evidence of compensation paid. They should also ensure that, regardless of their migration status, workers can at least access support, file complaints, and recover unpaid wages.

    “Workers know best what they have lost and what it will take to rebuild their lives,” de Rengervé remarked. “Companies and EU authorities should listen to affected workers and measure the efficiency of remediation by what workers receive and whether they completely remediate the harm suffered.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When Pakistani senators visited the prototype Islamabad Model Jail on November 19 and inspected the healthcare facilities that would be available to prisoners, they called them “adequate.” But the conditions they observed on their curated tour are a far cry from the reality most prisoners experience in Pakistan’s justice system.

    Recent findings suggest that human Rights Watch has documented structural and systemic problems in Pakistan’s jails and prisons that leave most inmates with little access to health care. Many inmates who fall ill in custody fail to receive prompt or decent care at all.

    After two prisoners died in Peshawar Central Prison following alleged delays in medical treatment, a lawyer petitioned the Peshawar High Court asking that prisons across the province be required to record when prisoners request medical help and establish clear procedures for emergency hospital transfers.

    Industry observers note that colonial-era laws have long-enabled Pakistani officials and powerful people to interfere in prison operations, sometimes making use of poor conditions to harass jailed political opponents. In a November 16 letter released by his lawyer, former Prime Minister Imran Khan appealed for urgent medical care for himself and his wife, Bushra Bibi, citing his high blood pressure and her need for eye surgery. Khan’s appeal echoes complaints about medical care in custody from former President Asif Ali Zardari and former Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif. All have alleged that prison services denied access to medical care as a form of punishment.

    According to recent reports, federal and provincial governments in Pakistan should bring health care in jails and prisons in line with international standards, notably the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (the Mandela Rules), which require that prisoners receive necessary free medical care to the same standard available in the community, with prompt attention in emergencies. In October, Justice Project Pakistan called for common standards across provinces so prisoners can see medical specialists when needed and continue treatment after release.

    Sources indicate that pakistan’s federal and provincial governments should provide prescribed medicines free of charge and require prisons to record how long patients wait for care. When care requires an urgent hospital transfer, prison authorities should promptly facilitate transport. Authorities should ensure all prisoners, regardless of political affiliation or status, receive timely and adequate medical care, with continuity of treatment.

    Modi’s Authoritarian Playbook in India.

    Impact of US Foreign Aid Cuts on HIV/AIDS Prevention and Care in Indonesia.
