    Latest Update: Free Education Is Key to Ending Child Marriage

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On November 27, the world marks the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage – a chance to end a practice that robs children of their childhood and prospects.
    • Free education is a powerful tool to help prevent it.
    • According to recent reports, and prevention needs to start earlier.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On November 27, the world marks the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage – a chance to end a practice that robs children of their childhood and prospects. Every year, 12 million girls are married before 18 – that’s one every three seconds.

    Free education is a powerful tool to help prevent it. UNICEF estimates that if all girls completed secondary education, it could cut child marriage by two-thirds. Yet school fees and indirect costs — uniforms, transport, books, examinations — force girls out of school and into early marriage. Free secondary education helps keep girls in school through adolescence, when the risk of child marriage is greatest. Evidence from 14 African countries shows that making lower secondary education free and compulsory raised girls’ educational attainment by 1.6 years.

    According to recent reports, and prevention needs to start earlier. A study published this month, covering women across 117 countries, found that legal guarantees of pre-primary education were associated with higher rates of school completion among girls and lower rates of child marriage and adolescent childbearing. Yet UNESCO reports that only 68 percent of countries and 46 percent of low-income countries legally guarantee tuition-free pre-primary education.

    Free education from pre-primary through secondary forms a continuous pathway to opportunity and empowerment.

    Sierra Leone shows what political leadership can achieve on both fronts. Its First Lady spearheaded this International Day, while its education ministers and diplomats have championed a fresh treaty on free education at the United Nations. Domestically, it has guaranteed 13 years of free education, from pre-primary through secondary, since 2023 and banned child marriage in 2024.

    Sources indicate that international law needs to catch up. The Convention on the Rights of the Child neither explicitly recognizes a right to early childhood care and education nor guarantees free pre-primary and secondary education for all. Sierra Leone, the Dominican Republic, Bulgaria and ten other countries are therefore advancing a fresh Optional Protocol to close these gaps. A binding commitment would strengthen accountability and drive national reforms. Negotiations on this proposed treaty will continue in October 2027.

    Industry observers note that on this inaugural International Day, Sierra Leone, supported by 14 countries, will bring diplomats, experts, and child advocates together in Geneva. Investing in free education advances girls’ rights, dignity, and futures – and is a decisive step towards ending child marriage. By supporting the Optional Protocol at the United Nations, states will be making a clear statement that they stand against child marriage and are committed to delivering a freer and fairer world for girls.

    • Slow Horses, the wonderful television series based on Mick Herron’s wonderful Slough House books series has been renewed.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Featured image credit:  Jack English/Apple TV+ via Rolling Stone.

    According to recent reports, yes. Slow Horses, the wonderful television series based on Mick Herron’s wonderful Slough House books series has been renewed. Season 6 just aired this fall, on its home network of Apple TV+, and work on the 7th season has begun.

    According to recent reports, but the series has been renewed even further than that. When Season 6 aired, we learned that the show had been renewed for an 8th season. This was great news.

    It has been revealed that and now, Apple has declared that the series will continue through Season 10! Yes, Seasons 9 and 10 have been announced! This means we have four more seasons to look forward to. That’s four more years of Jackson Lamb and his crew of misfits. That’s a whole American presidential term’s worth of Slow Horses.

    Industry observers note that until Season 6, each season of the show has adapted a single one of Heron’s novels, all in chronological order. Season 6 broke the mold by adapting two: the sequential volumes Joe Country and Slough House. This means there are two extant novels left to adapt, Bad Actors and Clown Town, and early reports have confirmed that seasons 7 and 8 will undertake each of those novels, respectively. This means that Heron’s next novel will also be guaranteed a season, as will the next.

    Will he indeed write more? Yes, it certainly seems so, though there have been no announcements about a newly introduced installment. The most recent novel, Clown Town, was released in 2025, and Heron’s novels typically have a 1-3 year gap in between them. But there’s still plenty of relevant Slough House material rife for adaptation; Heron has also published five Slough House novellas, none of which have been adapted yet. (Interested readers should note that all the novellas thus far have been collected in a volume called Standing By the Wall.).

    According to recent reports, the series Slow Horses stars Gary Oldman as the irascible, perpetually-disheveled, foul-mouthed, flatulent and yet thoroughly lovable MI5 agent Jackson Lamb, who oversees a notorious departmental backwater of the Secret Service called Slough House, an institutional repository for agents who have badly messed up (or pissed off somebody important). Time and time again Lamb and his team of oddballs, including Jack Lowden’s put-in-Slough-House-by-sabotage River Cartwright, wind up using their special skills, disregard for the rules, and occasional desire to prove themselves/not be messed with to save the day, often. It’s the best.

    It has been revealed that olivia Rutigliano is an Editor at Lit Hub and CrimeReads. Her other work appears in Vanity Fair, Vulture, Lapham's Quarterly, AirMail, the Los Angeles Review of Books, Public Books, The Baffler, Bright Wall/Dark Room, Politics/Letters, The Toast, Truly Adventurous, and elsewhere. She has a PhD from the departments of English/comparative literature and theatre at Columbia University, where she was the Marion E. Ponsford fellow. She hosts the podcasst "Culture Schlock" at Lit Hub Radio. She is on instagram at @oldebean, twitter at @oldrutigliano, and bluesky at @oliviarutigliano.bsky.social.

    Latest Update: A Study In Red, White and Blue: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle in the USA

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When I was choosing the setting for my newly introduced book, The Mark of Moriarty, which re-imagines the titular Professor survived his last battle with Sherlock Holmes, I found myself genuinely spoiled for choice.

    • He can go anywhere in the world except his homeland.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When I was choosing the setting for my newly introduced book, The Mark of Moriarty, which re-imagines the titular Professor survived his last battle with Sherlock Holmes, I found myself genuinely spoiled for choice.

    According to recent reports, holmes, for all his fantastical adventures, rarely travelled beyond London, glimpsing the wider world only when it came to his doorstep. Professor Moriarty, presumed dead post-Reichenbach and presumably still notorious in the UK, is in the exact opposite position.

    He can go anywhere in the world except his homeland.

    Industry observers note that while I was scouring the globe for an interesting place to send the master criminal, I kept coming back to a recurring theme in Sir Arthur Conan Doyle’s books. Indeed, even as a child, reading the classic Holmes adventures, one thought kept jumping out at me….

    “Wow, this guy really likes the USA.”.

    As I grew up, I discovered just how true this is. Sir Arthur Conan Doyle’s enthusiasm with the United States was a matter of public record. He took great inspiration from this newfound nation, recovering from a civil war and forging its future before his eyes.

    In the process of looking into this transatlantic fascination, I thought I’d share some weird and wonderful findings about Doyle’s brushes with the states, his encounters with citizens of that nation…  and one confrontation with a visitor from Atlantis.

    Sources indicate that even before he set foot in the States, Doyle devoured news from America. In fact, factions and societies from the USA featured prominently throughout his work and across the Sherlock Holmes canon.

    Industry observers note that when he was just twenty-one years old, Doyle anonymously published “An American’s Tale”, a short story in which an Englishman is accused of murdering a rival in Arizona. Taking the Englishman to “Flytrap Gulch” to hang him for his crime, the supposed victim is unexpectedly discovered inside… a giant man-eating plant.

    One of Doyle’s more fantastical tales, it certainly paints the USA as a strange and undiscovered country.

    As he embarked on the Holmes canon, Doyle still injected America into his stories, with a particular interest in the factions and societies across the pond.

    According to recent reports, his story, “The Five Orange Pips” features allusions to the infamous KKK. His final of the Sherlock Holmes novels, The Valley of Fear, was born out of his fascination with the Molly Maguires, a secret society that engaged in radical industrial action against Pennsylvanian mining companies, and the Pinkertons, the brutal detective agency who were hired to stop them.

    Doyle’s enthusiasm for American goings-on did sometimes outpace his knowledge, however, particularly due to his reliance on secondary sources which filtered to the UK.

    Holmes’ very first appearance, A Study In Scarlet, featured an organisation called the Danites, an avenging division of the Mormon Church’s mysterious “Council of Four”.

    While the Danites certainly existed, historians consider them a short-lived faction based in mid-century Missouri, and far from the organised assassin squad from the book, with Doyle’s own daughter explaining that her father “would be the first to admit that his first Sherlock Holmes novel was full of errors about the Mormons”.

    For the record, there’s no evidence that he believed in man-eating plants.

    Eventually, shortly after Sherlock met his end at the Reichenbach Falls, Sir Arthur Conan Doyle finally visited America for the first time.

    The Sherlock Holmes stories had proceeded him. He was met with an incredible reception from his already prominent U.S. fanbase, with the Boston Globe reporting him as; well proportioned, attractive and with a handsome face.

    In his journeys, Arthur Conan Doyle only grew fonder of America; reporting an incredible time spent on an elevator in Manhattan’s Woolworth Building, whose speed he compared to an artillery weapon, and defending the USA against nitpicking critics by saying;.

    “Every globe-trotter has paragraphs about the number of spittoons in a hotel bar (as if it matters!)”.

    Doyle also fell in love with the sport of baseball, to the point of committing a cardinal sin for any Brit; suggesting British football teams should adopt the sport.

    “I will venture to say, that if this was done, we should in a few years have as many to see a baseball final between Tottenham Hotspur and Preston North End as come now to the football.

    As to the furore which a decent British team, could we evolve one, would create in America, it is impossible to exaggerate it.”.

    Sadly, the United Kingdom has failed to assemble Doyle’s dream team.

    Despite the international success of his books, it was his forays into Spiritualism which brought Doyle back to the United States in the 1920’s, and which brought him in contact with his most prominent trans-atlantic friendship.

    One of the dramas that marked Doyle’s later American travels was his fractious friendship with magician Harry Houdini.

    According to recent reports, admirers of each other’s work, Doyle and Houdini held the opposite opinions on the supernatural that one might expect. Doyle, the creator of super-logician Sherlock Holmes, had become a devout spiritualist, while the magician Houdini was an ardent sceptic.

    Strangely enough, so strong was Doyle’s belief, that he insisted Houdini’s escapist tricks involved some form of magic, refusing to budge when Houdini himself told him otherwise.

    “My dear chap.” Doyle wrote in a letter to his friend. “Why do you go around the world seeking a demonstration of the occult when you are giving one all the time?”.

    Houdini even invited Doyle to the annual dinner at the Society of American Magicians. As a prank, and to prove Magicians could be fooled as much as they claimed Spiritualists were, Doyle screened footage of “live dinosaurs” to an astounded audience.

    These live dinosaurs would prove to be stop-motion animations, taken from the upcoming film adaptation of Doyle’s novel; The Lost World.

    Despite their spirited back and forth, tensions between the pair came to a head during a 1922 visit to Atlantic City, where Doyle’s wife Jean, channelled Houdini’s mother at a séance. The incident forced Houdini to publicly denounce the events in question, placing Doyle & Houdini publicly at odds.

    It was on his Spiritualism tour that Doyle had the strangest encounter Doyle he would perhaps have in America, when Doyle met one of his fans, an old Colonel from the South.

    While in Cleveland, described unflatteringly by Doyle as “a grim city of iron and shipping”, Doyle was advancing his lectures on Spiritualism, when he was confronted by an old Southern Colonel with an incredible story to tell.

    “The Colonel thought he was an Atlantean by origin,” Doyle reported, with the Colonel continuing to explain that his mother was the former Atlantean Queen.

    Though the author tolerated this eccentric visitor in the daytime, when the Colonel highlighted up at his hotel room at night, with a message from the former Queen, Doyle was forced to confront the more troubling side of fandom.

    In the end, long after Doyle’s love-affair with the USA began, Sherlock Holmes himself finally set foot in the States.

    It was in 1917, in “The Final Bow”, the last story in the Sherlock Holmes canon, that the detective confirmed he had crossed the Atlantic, travelling to Chicago and beyond.

    It’s a fitting end to a canon which, despite taking place primarily in London, is so deeply suffused with Doyle’s love for the States.

    The more I’ve learned about it, the more of a privilege it has seemed, to get the chance to send the iconic Professor to 1890’s New York.

    A place full of the societies, mysticism and people his creator adored so much, where he’ll pull in to the same dock that Sir Arthur Conan Doyle did when he first set foot in America.

    Jack Anderson is a UK-based writer of horror and mystery fiction. Jack got his start writing for the internet, penning the viral serial "Has Anyone Heard of the Left/Right Game?," which he wrote in a caffeine-fueled haze. It has since been adapted into a hit QCODE podcast starring Tessa Thompson in the leading role of Alice. His debut thriller, The Grief Doctor, was published by Raven Books in June 2024. Jack is also developing a number of original television and film ideas across the horror genre. He lives with his wife in Sheffield. Lifelong fans of games and puzzles, together they’re burning through every escape room in the North of England.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 23, 2026, 10:36 am CST.

    According to recent reports, then-White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks during a news briefing Oct. 13, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images).

    A former White House press secretary for President Donald Trump—whose tenure lasted five days in October—is facing an investigation by the State Bar of California after describing herself as a lawyer without being licensed to practice law.

    Sources indicate that katie Zacharia, who graduated with a JD from the Pepperdine University Rick J. Caruso School of Law in 2011, never passed the bar but has repeatedly referred to herself as a lawyer. A California code claims a candidate must have passed the bar exam to be called a lawyer.

    Zacharia has mentioned she worked as the outside counsel to the World Bank, an international financial institution, and as the general counsel for a conservative California nonprofit, according the Campaign for Accountability, a nonprofit government watchdog group.

    The Campaign for Accountability received a notice of the probe in a Thursday letter from the state bar and told the nonprofit that its complaint was assigned to an investigator and legal adviser.

    “Zacharia may have thought she was just playing a lawyer on TV, but by repeatedly holding herself out as an attorney on news programs, she was pretending to have authority she lacks,” remarked Michelle Kuppersmith, the executive director of the Campaign for Accountability, in a statement Thursday.

    Katie Zacharia out as White House press secretary.

    New White House press secretary calls confusion over legal credentials misunderstanding.

    Sources indicate that is she or isn’t she? Trump’s newly introduced press secretary claims she took the bar—in China.

    #158829. Latest Update: Quinn Connor on body horror, queerness, academia, and southern gothic novels

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3691 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Quinn Connor on body horror, queerness, academia, and southern gothic novels

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3691 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Your Beloved Remains is the third novel by Quinn Connor, and sits alongside their other Southern gothic stories.
    • After discovering the school might be closing, Celia finds a lost manuscript by the school’s founder, a feminist writer and heiress whose life and work has cast a long shadow over the school and its reputation.
    • The book is part mystery, part gothic horror, part dark academia, part dysfunctional romance, though that doesn’t do justice to the strangeness of the book, the atmosphere, the ideas around literature and the university that are thrown around—and just how much fun it all is.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Your Beloved Remains is the third novel by Quinn Connor, and sits alongside their other Southern gothic stories. This novel is set at Basin College, a small school in a remote part of Arkansas where Celia Kiel, the school’s archivist, has spent her whole life.

    After discovering the school might be closing, Celia finds a lost manuscript by the school’s founder, a feminist writer and heiress whose life and work has cast a long shadow over the school and its reputation. Working from a partial manuscript she found pickled in formaldehyde, she teams up with Joan Harriot, a literature postdoc, who is not just a gifted mimic but Celia’s academic nemesis, to forge and reconstruct the book in an effort to save the school.

    The book is part mystery, part gothic horror, part dark academia, part dysfunctional romance, though that doesn’t do justice to the strangeness of the book, the atmosphere, the ideas around literature and the university that are thrown around—and just how much fun it all is.

    The book tells the story of a very dysfunctional pair writing a manuscript, and so we reached out to Dr. Robyn Barrow and Alex Cronin, the writing duo behind Quinn Connor to ask about how they write together without trying to kill each other, academia, queer Southern stories, body horror, and how their writing surprises the people who know them.

    According to recent reports, AD: I really enjoyed Your Beloved Remains, which was so much fun. Maybe fun is the wrong word?

    AD: From the beginning of your writing career, I’m sure people have asked, how do the two of you work together? Here you have written a book that is explicitly about a literary partnership. Was this kind of inevitable?

    According to recent reports, AC: It probably was a little bit inevitable, because it’s always been interesting to us. Just promptly on the way we work: We’ve been doing this for thirteen years now. The way it works is that I have a character, Robyn has a character, and then we bring them in conversation. We are often literally passing the laptop back and forth, line by line, switching who writes it. So it ends up being super seamless.

    Of course, over thirteen years, I think we have learned enough about it to know how bad it could be if we did not truly like each other. We have strong boundaries with co-writing. We get along. We have a lot of the same tastes. We love each other. These are the things that make co-writing safe.

    But because it’s so safe for us, it was really fun to explore [the question], “but what if it wasn’t safe?” Because it is so vulnerable to be co-writing and sharing a creative project. To share that can feel really scary. So what if the worst thing happened? What if all of those hurt feelings that could exist grew into something wild and terrifying?

    AD: There is a scene where, not to spoil too much, but Celia gets those first pages back and she goes, this is horrible. Because she can’t give or take criticism well. But she’s also in pain because it’s so good and she knows she could never have written it, so she’s overwhelmed by anger and jealousy.

    AC: Robyn and I are very lucky because we have similar standards and we have similar but different talents. We’re very compatible, but co-writing with someone who is not compatible would be really difficult. Celia finds herself in this position where she just is struggling to keep up and that is a horror for her because she wants to be the keeper of Beatrice. The keeper of this archive and of her voice. And she can’t do it. The way that Harriot describes it is Celia is “a high priestess who can’t hear the voice of god.”.

    AD: Which is such a great phrase, but the book resembles a lot of different genres. It’s gothic, it’s dark academia. Robyn, I know you work in academia, so I’m sure you have thoughts on the genre.

    Industry observers note that RB: We have always loved Donna Tartt and The Secret History. We loved it and around 2017, 2018, it felt like suddenly the internet discovered it. It was everywhere and it sort of ballooned into this whole genre, “dark academia.”.

    In a recent development, it’s great that there are so many people enjoying reading and writing this genre, but it has gone quite far from The Secret History. Now there’s dark academic fantasy and all these versions that, to me, have nothing to do with academia. They’re not really exploring the themes of the university that I find interesting.

    When I pitched the idea for Your Beloved Remains to Alex, I was like, “We’re gonna make this call from inside the house.” This is about academic frustration. The kind of rage that can build up in an eternal grad program.

    When I came up with the pitch, I was in the sixth year of an eight-year grad program. A lot of Harriot’s struggles with her career and the feelings that she has about being a postdoc, was cathartic for me to write through. Hopefully it gets back to some of the roots of dark academia. We’re re-coining this book as “academic horror.”.

    In a recent development, AC: I’m just going to parrot what I’ve heard Robyn say before, which is that often these books focus on the students, but in our book, the students are not really a part of it. It’s about the institution. The students can leave on holiday break. They get to go home. This is about the people that don’t leave. Where the university is their life. Which, for Robyn, has been a really good thing.

    RB: It’s funny because since I wrote the book, I have gone on to finish my PhD and get a tenure-track job, which is like winning the lottery. That was never in the cards for Harriot. Harriot was never destined for tenure. [laughs].

    Sources indicate that AC: It’s kind of the same thing as the collaboration question. It’s an exploration of the dark side and the horrible “what if things had gone a different way.”.

    AD: There’s an exchange in the book. “What does it mean to want something so much you end up destroying it?” Harriot answers “it sounds like doing a PhD in the humanities.”.

    RB: [laughs] Exactly! Sometimes you make the thing that you love your job, which I would say is true both in academia and as an author. You make writing that you love the thing that you make money off of, and then you spend so long grinding that you actually ruin it. Harriot is so burnt out. She clearly came to being a literary scholar because she loved reading, and now she’s so cynical and so lost because of all the years of struggle with that.

    AD: You said that students are kind of the point of academia, but they’re only there for a few years, but there are people who spend their whole lives there.

    RB: Since most people who write books about academia have only ever been undergraduate students, they see themselves as the center of the system. But they’re really the compensatory engine of a system that is producing something that is actually not their education. I think that is fascinating. I truly care so much about my students. My students are the reason I want to be in academia, but for many researchers and faculty members, students are not the reason that they are doing their job.

    AC: Also, the people who run the college, the board and the President, they’re looking at the bottom line. There’s this question that’s the propulsive engine of the first act: Is Basin College going to close? Celia cares because of the archive and because it’s her home. But there’s also the question of what about all of these students that are right now there. What’s going to happen to them?

    Industry observers note that there is this unspoken understanding that the board doesn’t care about them. It’s not about them. They’re a part of this system and nobody is thinking about them at all.

    AD: They’re running a business.

    Industry observers note that RB: The book was coming out of a moment when it felt like universities were operating as these hedge funds for the wealthy. We started writing this book in 2023. Now higher education is under threat. I think that the university is a really good and important thing in our society. I want to defend it and I want to be a good voice in the university.

    According to recent reports, AC: I think there’s a major question in the book, “how do you love something?” Celia’s version of loving it is excusing any of its wrongs and pretending it’s perfect. Harriot’s version is critiquing it almost to the point of picking it apart.

    Recent findings suggest that I think that’s how we feel about the university. Yes, it’s wonderful. It’s something that we need. It also is worthy of critique and could be improved and made better. There are these questions of how you engage with something that you love, and because you love it you are frustrated by it greatly.

    According to recent reports, AD: Historically most universities were set apart from cities to let people study and work. And there’s a way that attracts people like Celia who use it as a place to hide from the larger world.

    RB: It’s got a monastic quality. That can also go into a cult-like quality. Harriot is really running from her past by arriving at Basin College, which is a very particularly isolated and spooky version.

    AD: It is very remote, but also, there are a lot of colleges in the middle of nowhere.

    Industry observers note that AC: Beatrice Donahue created it specifically for that reason. She said, “my husband is finally dead, I have money, I am free. I want to go do exactly what I want to do.”.

    What she wanted to do was find some place remote where she and the women in her life and her lover could be themselves in all of their weird, witchy, queer glory. A lot of universities were not created for that reason, but it was fun to think about this university that was and how these things can start from such a seed and still become so institutionalized and twisted and different from the starting place.

    It has been revealed that RB: I do like that point that Basin College in its foundational message, was meant to be a safe place for women and a safe place for queer people to live as their true selves. I feel like the university can be that way. The ivory tower is a place where you see many different kinds of people getting to ask the kinds of questions they’re interested in. I feel like that is a beautiful thing about college. But it all depends on who’s in charge.

    AD: It does get at that, which is so important for people. Also it touches on how a lot of schools that may have become institutions, but were started by people who were strange or even crazy.

    AC: [laughs] Beatrice is, but she’s gloriously powerful. She’s dead but she has cast such a long shadow. She brought these women who did not fit in society. One of our inspirations was Victorian tea rooms, which was one of the few jobs back then that women could have. So Beatrice had a tea room. Women were finding ways to exist and to be free under incredible constraints. That’s what Basin College was for her.

    AD: It’s a queer book about how queer spaces have always existed just as queer people have always existed. And that these spaces and institutions have existed through time.

    Sources indicate that RB: This is our third novel and in our previous work we’ve had queer storylines that have been a reclaiming of queer joy, which has been really wonderful. In this book we wanted to just have freaky scary lesbians doing bad things and not apologizing for it. Just ripping the world down.

    AC: There’s all sorts of different ways that queer people can be portrayed. Because they’re people. You almost have to start with a portrayal where they are good, because there are a lot of people that may not have knowingly met a queer person. You almost have to start with, guess what, you can love a queer character. The more these stories come out, the more freedom you have to add grittiness and reality into that portrayal.

    It’s wonderful to be able to have queer characters that behave badly and it doesn’t feel like a condemnation on queerness as an entire experience. For us, being able to write through queer joy gave us the freedom to write queer messiness as well.

    RB: This is coming from our background as Southern women, as well. I feel like up in these parts it can feel that queer pain is a distant memory for many people, but for us, coming out in 2018 was a completely different world. Writing Southern stories about queer people means a lot to people in Arkansas and these places.

    AC: There’s people that would have you believe that queerness doesn’t exist there. Or that it needs to be kept very quiet, or regulated extremely heavily. Or made illegal. But there have always been queer people in Arkansas.

    Sources indicate that there’s also the idea that the North is the home of the ivory tower. That Fresh England is where you’ve got all these schools, but there’s always been incredible intelligence like in Arkansas. These things, that they would have you believe don’t exist, have always been there. These people, that they tell you don’t exist or don’t deserve to exist, have always been there and been a part of it.

    According to recent reports, AD: As you were talking about the messiness, I keep thinking about how the book takes place over a few months. It opens with the fall semester and the school is functioning as it has been, and by the Christmas holiday, everything unravels and descends into chaos.

    In a recent development, RB: We have Beatrice Donahue’s dark secret at the center of the novel. You don’t find out right away, which has made it hard for me at times to know how to pitch the novel. I feel like this is a key element that you don’t want to spoil. Beatrice lost her lover and the aftermath of that grief and where she goes with that is super kinky and interesting and transgressive and queer.

    Then you have these women in the 1980s that are excavating that and discovering within themselves how they feel about that and how they feel about each other. It’s fun to surprise the reader with that part way through. It’s good to highlight for readers that the book is spicy and bizarre. And a great time, hopefully.

    Recent findings suggest that AC:  We’re thinking about all of these highfalutin ideas, but we’re also playing a game of chicken with each other. We’re trying to freak each other out a little bit when we’re writing. We’re trying to make it fun.

    Sometimes I write something and then I’m sitting there waiting for Robin to get to it so I can get her reaction. There’s a lot about the book that is intentionally fun because we were having fun. Everything that the reader feels, we felt as we were writing it and surprising each other and grossing each other out and delighting each other.

    AD: I’m sure. Going, what if she cuts her foot, what if it gets infected, what if we have this body horror scene.

    AC: What’s weird is that we wrote all of that, but it grosses me out to think about it. One of my friends was reminding me about a particular scene with the foot. I remember us writing that, and I have not gone back and read it again because it grosses me out! [laughs].

    AD: I’m pretty sure I know the exact scene you’re talking about.

    AC: [laughs] It’s a weird way to feel about something you wrote.

    AD: At the center of the book is this lost manuscript of Beatrice’s, and in writing the book you had to figure out how much of that book to write, how much to include so it doesn’t overwhelm the story.

    AC: A couple people have asked about this, actually. One friend remarked, “you should do Dreams of the Rose, the entire book from Beatrice Donahue.” Our answer has consistently been, “no!” My gosh, that was so hard to do.

    RB: One of the massive influences in the book that I don’t think we’ve talked about before is Possession by A.S. Byatt. I love that novel. It’s absolutely amazing. In that book there’s a lot of the writing of the authors in the book.

    According to recent reports, with Beatrice Donahue we wanted the kind of unreachability of her to be center stage. What’s on the page is all of the writings of Beatrice Donahue that there is. There’s no additional pages. We found it extremely tiresome to do.

    According to recent reports, harriot has this power of mimicry where she can hear the writing of someone else and then produce it. That came from my own perception of my own writing. I feel like I can really get the sound of someone else’s writing and copy that or produce that, in a sense. Beatrice Donahue is a shared character, but I would read Mary Shelley and Poe and nineteenth-century work and then I would write these passages of Donahue.

    It has been revealed that I’m very attuned to word choice. I feel like it’s so easy to get taken out of that kind of writing with a misplaced word or something that just doesn’t hit quite right. This is just someone in the present pretending to write about the past. I wanted it to have a strong truth claim. Starting with the note from the editors and then all the writing, I wanted it to feel really immersive. This could have been true.

    According to recent reports, AD: You mentioned before that each were the primary writer of one of the characters. Who did you write?

    Recent findings suggest that AC: I wrote Celia. To the great surprise of most people, I wrote Celia.

    RB: For some reason, Alex’s friends were like, “she couldn’t have done that.”.

    Sources indicate that AC: I think because the wildness of Celia and where we go in her perspective is pretty stark. I think that a lot of people that know me are just surprised because I’m an introvert. There’s a lot that comes out in Celia’s perspective that people maybe didn’t think we were capable of, who have read our other books or know us personally.

    AD: I think Celia would have to be written by an introvert.

    Industry observers note that AC: That’s how I feel! She’s got a very rich inner world, and it’s twisted in there.

    AD: It’s also funny that you wrote the foot scene and then went, this is disgusting, I can’t read it again.

    RB: Alex writes way grosser stuff than I do.

    Sources indicate that AD: That is interesting. Do people have a somewhat misunderstood sense of what you write or how you write?

    According to recent reports, RB: I think there’s definitely a pattern between the three books. Alex’s characters are always extremely vulnerable and very emotionally open. Which is interesting because between the two of us, she’s definitely more emotionally unavailable in the real world. My characters are a bit more closed off and they’re usually cool. [laughs] I’m the least cool person, but then I write these cool characters. To my best friends, it’s pretty obvious that Harriot is me. She’s like my shadow side.

    In a recent development, people do have a good time guessing. We go back and forth, should we tell people who wrote what? Should we keep it a secret? Because obviously we want the experience to be seamless.

    In a recent development, AD: You mentioned one struggle has been finding a way to talk about the book without spoiling too much. Which I understand.

    It has been revealed that RB: I’ve been thinking about the pitch for the book and if we’re pitching it correctly. I think what it’s really about is that Celia longs for more than anything, the love of this Victorian author that she’s always admired. In her desperate reaching for that, she recruits her academic nemesis who has this talent for mimicry to go with her on this journey that leads to a total shit show descent into complete chaos in this snowy remote college.

    It has been revealed that that’s what I think the book is about. There’s many, many bizarre and spicy surprises along the way. [laughs].

    In a recent development, AD: It’s true, and a lot of what we’ve been talking about, the gothic elements and academia and the two falling for each other, that’s the first half. The second half, just buckle up for the ride.

    RB: Someone asked us, do you provide aftercare for your readers at the end of the book? I was like, we don’t. I feel like the book is just like a rock and roll roller coaster and you get spat out at the end. I hope that you’re sitting there, staring at the book going, what did I just read? [laughs].

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    At the time of the Latest Planchette article’s circulation in 1886, Charles Kennard was a real estate agent who owned a fertilizer business in Chestertown, Maryland, just across the wide expanse of the Chesapeake Bay from the state’s industrial center of Baltimore. Kennard was born in Delaware on Christmas Eve, 1857, and was eleven years old when he witnessed the “wonderful workings of Planchette” during its ﬁrst great craze. By 1876, he had begun “an investigation of psychical phenomenon” while living in Philadelphia, and his table-rapping experiments continued after he moved to Chestertown that same year.

    While Kennard never acknowledged any inﬂuence of the Ohio talking-board reports that appeared in 1886, it was that same year he claimed he envisioned an identical breakthrough, imagining he could receive communications quicker than raps or automatic writing “if words could be spelled by the alphabet.” He struck on what he believed was an original idea: “In 1886 I made a crude board, using a cake board and a table with four legs and a pointer, marking the alphabet and numerals in pencil,” and used the pairing to autonomously spell out messages letter by letter, joining the ranks of Armstrong, Damon, and Long as one of the earliest- known talking-board creators.

    To reﬁne his primitive eﬀorts, Kennard claimed, he visited local cabinetmaker and undertaker Ernest Christian “E. C.” Reiche, a Prussian immigrant whose workshop was adjacent to Kennard’s oﬃce in Chestertown’s Voshell House. He commissioned “about a dozen boards a little neater in appearance than the cake board,” which he then oﬀered for sale locally. He claimed his boards were “always being borrowed by neighbors, and those who purchased the few wanted more,” echoing similar stirrings of interest in Ohio that same year.

    By his own account, he petitioned Reiche to continue the productive partnership, but as Kennard later recalled, “I asked him to continue making them for me and we would put the board on the market. This he mentioned he would not do. He was too busy to make any more. I would have to get someone else.” Left without a craftsman to manufacture the boards, Kennard’s commercial ambitions sat temporarily idle.

    Three years later, a competitive marketplace took its toll on Kennard’s fertilizer business, and in February 1890, he relocated his family to Baltimore. There, he opened a upcoming real estate oﬃce in the Barnum Building and established new headquarters for his fertilizer organization at 220 S. Charles Street. Kennard also rekindled his ambition to commercialize a talking board.10 In an account that echoes Cyrus H. Farley’s attempts to pitch planchettes in Boston, Kennard “revealed the board to several who could see nothing of the future in it.”.

    But a fortuitous meeting came with local attorney and fellow Freemason Elijah Jeﬀerson Bond, who took an intense interest in what he called Kennard’s “witch board.” Bond recounted in later years how he made “vital improvements” to Kennard’s design to get it into “marketable shape,” which included a round planchette with a sharply pointed extension that served as an indicator, setting it far apart from the heart-shaped planchettes of yesteryear. He paired the fresh planchette with a board that included two arched rows of the alphabet with a straight line of numbers below, closely matching newspaper illustrations from 1886.

    According to recent reports, bond added embellishments, including a black dot representing the full moon in one upper corner and a crescent moon in the other, and black stars in the bottom corners. An illustration at the bottom center depicting two men shaking hands—an crucial symbol of fraternity among Freemasons—ﬂanked on each side with the conjunction “Good Bye.”.

    The pair partnered with the goal of patenting and manufacturing the idea, with Bond ﬁnancing their earliest eﬀorts with a $500 investment.

    The duo’s latest talking board had not yet been christened with its iconic name. As the two ironed out the details of the patent design in April 1890, they assembled at Bond’s home with some of his family members. Not satisﬁed with the initial name they had chosen, Charles Kennard proposed they ask the board what it would like to be called, as he later recounted:.

    According to recent reports, the name Ouija was adopted by Mr. Bond and myself. We called this board by another name until we could secure a better one. One evening about April 1890, while trying the board with a Miss Peters, Mr. Bond’s sister-in-law, in the large boarding house at that time on the corner of Charles and Centre streets, where Mr. Bond boarded, I remarked that we had not yet settled upon a name, and as the board had helped us in other ways, we would ask it to propose one. It spelled out O-U-I-J-A. When I asked the meaning of the word it noted “Good Luck.”.

    Industry observers note that miss Peters there upon drew upon her neck a chain which had at the end a locket, on it a ﬁgure of a woman and at the top the word “Ouija.” We asked her if she had thought of the name, and she said she had not. We then adopted the word.

    Sources indicate that ouija was a strange word seemingly without precedent, and its fascinating combination of consonants and vowels, fabricated through Peters’s mediumship, added to the board’s mystique, even as unlikely as it was to have appeared on a locket. Yet her locket is an vital clue that her role in Ouija’s naming may have direct ties to the Spiritualist movement.

    Recent findings suggest that peters had no known connection to Spiritualism in her upbringing, but such influence was deeply rooted in her future husband and then suitor Ernest Herbert Donisthorpe Nosworthy. An immigrant from the UK who arrived in January 1888 to work as a traveling salesman, Nosworthy was the seventh child of Frederick Arthur and Eliza Louisa Spry Nosworthy, née Thompson, of Manchester, England, the latter of whom was a talented trance medium who “often attracted large and refined public audiences at Birkenhead by her dramatic powers.”.

    According to recent reports, she was the daughter of George Thompson, himself a prominent Spiritualist who sat with Leah Fox in the United States, and had served on the Council of the British National Association of Spiritualists. The younger Nosworthy’s sister, Beatrice, was also regarded as “one of the youngest and one of the best of trance mediums” in England.

    The Nosworthy family’s close bonds with one of the most famous mediums of the era may have directly influenced Ouija’s name. The family hosted famous medium Cora Hatch when she visited England, living with them for months at a time on multiple occasions during Nosworthy’s formative school years. Eliza Nosworthy was considered Hatch’s herald and was so close to the family that when Eliza’s prominent father died, the medium adopted him as a newly introduced spirit guide with the blessing of the Nosworthy clan.

    However, it was another of Hatch’s spirit guides who might have inspired Ouija’s name: the specter of a woman named Ouina, Cora Scott’s most famous contact for her trance mediumship, and Spiritualists considered her a generous spirit who acted as “a messenger of peace and love between the two worlds.” Exposure to Ouina was most certainly in the environment of Ernest Nosworthy’s upbringing, and it may explain the mysterious locket with a woman’s figure and name described by Kennard in his remembrance of Ouija’s naming.

    Whatever the case, Bond and Kennard adopted the enigmatic moniker and turned toward securing a patent for their newly named product.

    During the mid-1930s, more stories of deaths involving messages received through Ouija made the headlines of American newspapers. The first involved the Turley family of Arizona, when fifteen-year-old Mattie shot her father, Ernes, twice in the back with a shotgun, which resulted in his death a few weeks later.

    In a recent development, the news spread far beyond local publications when reports revealed that it was Ouija’s messages that had commanded Mattie to murder her father. The story was further sensationalized by news that her mother and Ernest’s wife, Dorothea, was once voted “the most beautiful girl in America.”.

    Recent findings suggest that widely reprinted articles revealed how Dorothea had become obsessed with a local “handsome cowboy” named Kent Pearce and used the Ouija to manipulate her daughter into murdering her own father so that Dorothea would be free to marry Pearce. All three were charged, although Pearce denied any involvement and was ultimately found not guilty. Mattie pled guilty in juvenile court and was sentenced to an Arizona reform school, while her mother was found guilty and sentenced to prison but was freed three years later.

    In a recent development, another sensational Ouija murder involved the Hurd family of Kansas City in 1935. Family matriarch Nellie received messages through her Ouija that her seventy-seven-year-old husband, Herbert, was “too fond of another woman” and that he had given his secret lover “$15,000 of a hidden fortune.”.

    After receiving the messages, Nellie and her daughter Bertha ambushed Herbert and chained him to his bed before subjecting him to all manner of tortures, including beating him with a revolver, burning the soles of his feet with matches, and stabbing his legs with a dagger. Bertha also set to killing “the children”—three dogs and a cat—with carbon monoxide, which Nellie had commanded.

    These horrible acts led to Herbert signing a forced confession admitting to his affair, which the two women signed as “witnesses.” But a few hours later, Nellie momentarily left her gun within Herbert’s reach, and he seized it and shot his wife four times before making his escape.

    Police afterward discovered Herbert “running along the street clad only in his pajamas and carrying a still smoking revolver,” and he confessed to police immediately. Nellie died from her wounds, and the courts deter-mined her death to be a “justifiable homicide.” Bertha remained free after Herbert refused to press charges.

    As in prior decades, these Ouija-inspired murders sparked a flurry of sensational headlines like “The Ouija Again Spelled Death!” even if Herbert’s actions were an act of self-defense, and helped contribute to the growing chorus of Ouija’s malign and diabolical associations in the media.

    Recent findings suggest that david Brandon Hodge is the author ofSupernatural Machines: The History of Spirit Communication Devices. Hodge is a historian, collector, and author specializing in the history of spirit communication devices. Founder of MysteriousPlanchette.com and curator of the world’s largest archive of séance artifacts, his research has appeared in Smithsonian Magazine and Paranormal Review, and has served as a consultant for museums and exhibitions worldwide, including the acclaimed Supernatural America exhibit at the Minneapolis Institute of Art and the Peabody Essex Museum’s Conjuring the Spirit World exhibit. Hodge has also appeared in many prominent programs as an expert on the occult, including Oddities, Mysteries at the Museum, and Expedition Files, and served as historical consultant and provided séance artifacts for Rick Alverson’s film The Mountain and Lasse Hellström’s biopic Hilma. Hodge is also a respected game designer and lecturer, known for his horror-themed scenarios and his work with Atlas Obscura and Coast to Coast AM. He owns and operates Monkey See, Monkey Do! toy store and Major Top Candy Shop in Austin, Texas, where he lives with his two children, Jack and Elliot, and the ghosts of several cats.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that here are five newly translated works of crime fiction, featuring selfish tourists, corrupt cops, desperate horse racers, antiquities smugglers, and amateur sleuths. Enjoy!

    Yves Ravey, Taormina Translated by Alyson Waters (New York Review of Books).

    According to recent reports, taormina is a ruthless condemnation of our selfish modern era, a road trip novel in which a married couple on vacation in Italy run over a migrant child, then proceed to do….nothing. They do not check on the body. They do not go to the police. They do not accept any form of responsibility. They don’t even bother to cover up their crimes (or at least, they cover for themselves only lazily and ineptly). The only action available to either spouse, by dint of their warped world view, is to blame others for their problems. A vicious gem that wouldn’t feel out of place in mid-century noir, although the story’s catalysts are firmly grounded in the 21st century.

    Gustavo Eduardo Abrevaya, The Bullet Inside Me Translated by Andrea G Labinger ( Schaffner Press).

    The Bullet Inside Me takes places at the height of Argentina’s Secret War; in this hard-boiled thriller of compromise and conspiracy, the young daughter of a fascist functionary is kidnapped, in a case that threatens the entire dictatorial order. By the same author as the impressive Sanctuary, this one’s just as compelling, and just as vicious.

    Genki Kawamura, The Horse and I Translated by Chikako Kobayashi (Flatiron).

    Sources indicate that A beautiful tale of the lengths we go to for love. In The Horse and Me, a shy clerk forges a deep bond with a racing horse, one coveted by a wealthy rider who seems poised to destroy the stallion’s spirit. Without means of her own, the clerk begins stealing from her own union’s coffers in order to purchase, then maintain, her newfound soulmate. When her colleagues begin to catch on to the thefts, Kawamura’s heroine finds herself backed into a corner and desperate to turn her horse into a champion.

    Sacha Naspini, The Witch’s Mouth Translated by Clarissa Botsford  (Europa).

    Grave robbing in Tuscany from ancient Etruscan graves has been significant business since before the war, but with upcoming regulations cracking down on antiquities smuggling elsewhere in Italy, the little band of thieves at the center of the novel face new gangs trying to muscle into their territory, renewed inquiries from weary local authorities, and internal divisions that threaten to dissolve their operation entirely.

    Indrek Hargla, The Ghost of Rataskaevu Street Translated by Adam Cullen (Pushkin Press).

    Sources indicate that hargla’s second novel to feature apothecary Melchior, released for the first time in the US this month, takes his hero on a dark journey stretching far into the city’s past. When three different townspeople die just after seeing a ghost, the pharmacist and amateur sleuth decides to dig into the matter. In between brewing tinctures, infusing remedies, and proscribing his usual treatments, Melchior keeps circling back to a house in the center of town, once the setting of a terrible crime, and key to understanding the more recent killings.

She grew up in Austin and worked as a bookseller before becoming a Very Professional Internet Person. She lives in central Texas with her cat, Fritz Lang.

    Welcome to The Fashion Police, a column where we spotlight some of the best fashion in crime film and TV.

    It has been revealed that it’s true. The United States navy is retiring a its signature peacoat. Yes, its signature peacoat! “The double-breasted, hip-length wool peacoat that is synonymous with the romance of the sea.” They’re retiring an iconic garment, a staple not only of military fashion, but also of fashion in general.

    They are replacing it with a black, synthetic, all-weather parka. Why are they doing this? A statement from the Navy’s Uniform Board said that it was due to the Navy’s “commitment to eliminating unnecessary costs while ensuring sailors have the cold-weather protection they need to accomplish their missions.” The U.S. Naval Institute News revealed that it was chosen was chosen for its “modern appearance,” and “its versatility in being able to be worn with service and dress uniforms and civilian clothing.” But it has NO personality. This is like tearing down a historic 18th century townhouse to put up a glass and steel high rise.

    In her piece on this landmark decision, Vanessa Friedman at The Latest York Times noted the history and symbolic associations of the garment, writing.

    According to recent reports, first designed for Dutch sailors in the 18th century, the pijakker was particularly well-suited for life at sea: roomy enough to accommodate warm inner layers but streamlined enough not to get caught in a ship’s rigging. Its collar could be turned up to shield the face against wind, and side pockets kept the coat closer to the body in cold weather.

    Adopted by the Royal Navy in 1857, the peacoat made the leap to the U.S. Navy shortly thereafter, becoming standard issue in 1886. And though small details may have been tweaked, the general style has remained the same.

    In 1962, Friedman notes, Yves Saint-Laurent included a peacoat in his womenswear Rive-Gauche show, launching the coat as as style staple for women. According to the brand,.

    According to recent reports, the simple shape of this practical garment sculpted the silhouette. The fact that it was not fitted and covered the hips made it ideal for women who did not yet feel daring enough to wear pants, which accentuated the female form.

    Sources indicate that saint Laurent’s 1962 fashion show opened with the pea coat, which was the first piece he presented under his own name. The model wore it with white shantung pants and mules. This ensemble paved the way for Yves Saint Laurent’s signature style, which borrowed from menswear in order to make women feel comfortable and confident.

    Industry observers note that but, for our purposes, the most iconic use of the peacoat is Robert Redford’s look in Three Days of the Condor, Sydney Pollack’s 1975 political espionage thriller, based on James Grady’s novel Six Days of the Condor). Redford plays a low-level CIA employee in New York City who is the sole survivor of an attack on his small office branch, and then goes on the run, attempting to untangle what appears to be an enormous intra-bureau conspiracy. The peacoat is a nice choice for this character; as Valerie Steele, the director of the Museum at the Fashion Institute of Technology told The New York Times, “the peacoat doesn’t have the associations with violence and warfare often attached to camouflage and Army greatcoats. Rather, the peacoat more often represents bravery against the elements and the romance of voyages to places unknown.”.

    #158823. Jessica Hamilton on possession, menopause, and the horrors of middle age

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1189 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Jessica Hamilton on possession, menopause, and the horrors of middle age

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1189 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Demonic possession or plain old menopause?
    • Industry observers note that in my novel, The Woods, my protagonist, Alice, is in the throes of middle age.
    • In a recent development, scalding flames spread quickly up the chest, wrapping a burning hand around the neck, moving onto the face causing a sheen of sweat on the forehead and upper lip that only intensifies the burn—no escape is possible from the fire within.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Demonic possession or plain old menopause? It can be hard to tell, which is why the horrors of middle age for women lend themselves so well to the horror genre. There are the physical horrors, when our bodies betray us. There are the psychological ones, when our minds betray us. And there are the sociological ones, perhaps the most insidious of them all, when our own communities betray us.

    Industry observers note that in my novel, The Woods, my protagonist, Alice, is in the throes of middle age. So, while she’s sure something sinister is in the woods, which seems to be targeting her family, she also questions herself at every turn, is constantly doubted by those around, her all while powering through the many physical hurdles of menopause.

    In a recent development, scalding flames spread quickly up the chest, wrapping a burning hand around the neck, moving onto the face causing a sheen of sweat on the forehead and upper lip that only intensifies the burn—no escape is possible from the fire within. A description of an everyday hot flash and yet it reads like a scene in a horror novel of a person being burned alive. The same can be done for the rivers of blood that may run unabated, the headaches that feel like a metal stake being driven into the scalp, the withering of the skin, the clumps of hair found in the drain after showering, the crack and creak of joints that ache.

    In a recent development, these physical symptoms sound like well-known body horror tropes but are in fact real life experiences for many women going through menopause. In combination these symptoms can easily make a woman feel as though her body has been possessed by some evil force.

    In his novel, Mary, Nat Cassidy describes the physical struggles of his middle-aged protagonist, Mary, in such a visceral way that it is in itself the horror. Making the reader forget that this is a stage of life that all women go through and not just the fiction of a very adept horror author.

    Then there are the psychological impacts of middle age for women. Extreme fatigue, anxiety, unprovoked anger, incessant mental chatter, dark thoughts, disrupted sleep, sudden surges of unmanageable rage, untreatable depression, gaps in memory—I have heard many women complain of one or more of these symptoms due to menopause.

    Recent findings suggest that and yet, this list is what comes up when you google the symptoms of demonic possession. Clearly making the point that middle age lends itself well to the horror novel. It is one thing to feel that your body is turning on you, it’s another to feel that your mind is as well. And if you can’t trust yourself, then who can you trust?

    In the novel, Death in Her Hands by Ottessa Moshfegh the protagonist Vesta becomes obsessed with a note that she finds in the woods around her house and the mystery that it presents. Very rapidly the lines of reality become blurred for Vesta due to her confused state and her inability to decipher what is real and what is her own paranoia and delusion. She can’t trust herself which means she’s locked in an inescapable cycle of discovering something and then mistrusting that discovery.

    My own protagonist, Alice, senses that there is something sinister in the woods around their new home but is prone to second guessing her own intuition because she no longer feels as sure of her memory or perception as she once did, before middle age. She wants to assert herself and what she believes is happening but lacks the confidence to do so under the influence of menopause.

    Sources indicate that if you’re unable to trust your memory, if you’re prone to paranoia and anxiety, irrational mood swings and brain fog you’re also ripe to be gaslit by those around you. Women being gaslit is not a new concept. The diagnosis of hysteria, which women were given until it was removed from the DSM in1980, was perhaps the most powerful tool of gaslighting.

    Industry observers note that these days it’s a little less obvious but happens just the same. It’s easy to dismiss a middle-aged women’s feelings by claiming that they are caused my menopausal hormones. But, if the paranoia, anxiety, depression grief etc. are in fact rooted in something other than hormonal changes this leaves a woman without the support she actually needs.

    In the case of my protagonist, her concerns about the safety of her family and the threat of the woods are dismissed by her husband, mother and best friend as the ramblings of a paranoid, anxiety riddled, grief stricken menopausal woman. Add to this the fact that women often feel invisible in society after reaching middle age and it results in lack of credibility, power and presence. What could be worse than the horror of not being believed, not having any authority and not being seen?

    It has been revealed that why did I choose to write about a middle-aged woman experiencing menopause in my latest novel? I’m fifty-one years old and have begun to experience a lot of what my protagonist, Alice, experiences. I wanted to give a voice to this stage in life and hopefully create some empathy for it in readers.

    Recent findings suggest that mostly though, it was because the things that Alice was experiencing at this stage of life were great tools to ramp up the tension of the horror in my writing. A character filled with paranoia, anxiety, and sleeplessness from the very start of the novel. One who questions herself and is questioned by those around her and who causes the reader to question whether something is real or simply a paranoid delusion. Set this character in a house with a tragic history, surrounded by ancient woods and I was off to the races.

    Recent findings suggest that the simple truth is that often real life is the scariest of all and in the case of middle age for women, I’m sad to say, that is most certainly the case. Demonic possession or menopause? My bet is that it’s menopause. I don’t believe in demons, despite being a writer of horror.

    Fortunately, there’s hormone replacement therapy, an increase in information about it and the horror does, apparently, have an end at some point. In the meantime, may there be many more novels that have the menopausal hero saving the day, despite the hot flashes, brain fog, sleepless nights and gaslighting.

    It has been revealed that jessica Hamilton was born in Australia but grew up in Canada. She has lived and worked in the Czech Republic, Taiwan, India and Japan. She studied writing at the Humber School for Writers as well as George Brown College. She lives in Ontario, Canada with her husband, son and daughter. Her debut novel is titled What You Never Knew, her second novel is titled, Don't You Dare, and both are thrillers published by Crooked Lane Books.

    #158822. Justices to consider disputes over transgender servicemembers, E. Jean Carroll’s jury award, and acting U.S. attorneys at next private conference

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (979 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Justices to consider disputes over transgender servicemembers, E. Jean Carroll’s jury award, and acting U.S. attorneys at next private conference

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that the justices of the Supreme Court aren’t scheduled to meet for a private conference – and vote on upcoming petitions for review – for two-and-a-half weeks.
    • Industry observers note that the federal government and President Donald Trump are at the center of three of the biggest petitions for review up for consideration on Dec.
    • Talbott, the justices will decide whether to review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that bars the Trump administration from expelling several transgender servicemembers from the military.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that the justices of the Supreme Court aren’t scheduled to meet for a private conference – and vote on upcoming petitions for review – for two-and-a-half weeks. But when they do, on Friday, Dec. 4, they will have a number of high-profile cases to consider – which could, in turn, lead to a busy spring.

    Industry observers note that the federal government and President Donald Trump are at the center of three of the biggest petitions for review up for consideration on Dec. 4.

    In United States v. Talbott, the justices will decide whether to review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that bars the Trump administration from expelling several transgender servicemembers from the military.

    In the government’s petition for review, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer called the decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit “gravely erroneous” and argued that its “reasoning cannot be squared with this Court’s precedents or deference to the military.”.

    Industry observers note that the challengers urged the court to stay out of the dispute, calling the D.C. Circuit’s decision “narrow” and temporary. And in any event, they added, the ruling is correct, because the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers was motivated by hostility to transgender people rather than “military judgments.”.

    In another case to be considered, Trump and the federal government have each filed petitions for review in connection with Trump’s challenge to the $83.3 million verdict entered against him in a lawsuit brought by E. Jean Carroll, who had alleged that in 1996 Trump had sexually abused her in a dressing room at a New York department store and that Trump in 2019 had defamed her by calling her a liar.

    Trump’s petition for review points to the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Trump v. United States, in which it held that presidents generally have broad immunity for their acts while in office. Trump’s private attorney, Robert Giuffra, wrote that “[t]he threat of even a single damages judgment based on official acts will render all Presidents ‘unable to boldly and fearlessly carry out [their] duties for fear that [they] may be next.’”.

    The federal government’s petition for review asks the Supreme Court to also decide whether the federal government, rather than Trump, should be the defendant in Carroll’s case because Trump made the statements at the center of the dispute as part of his role as president.

    And in United States v. Jackson and United States v. Office of the New York State Attorney General, the justices will decide whether to weigh in on the legality of Trump’s appointments of acting U.S. attorneys in Nevada and New York.

    It has been revealed that under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, the federal law that governs how the executive branch can temporarily staff vacant positions that require presidential appointment and confirmation by the Senate, interim officers can serve for 120 days. Under that law, then-Attorney General Pamela Bondi appointed Sigal Chattah as the interim U.S. Attorney for the District of Nevada, effective April 1, 2025, after Jason Frierson, who was nominated by then-President Joe Biden, stepped down.

    With only a few days remaining before her interim appointment was set to expire, Chattah resigned, and Bondi designated her as the first assistant U.S. attorney. In that post, Bondi remarked, Chattah would have the power under the FVRA “to serve as Acting United States Attorney upon a vacancy in that office.” Bondi also gave Chattah the powers of a U.S. attorney for legal proceedings in Nevada.

    Bondi followed a similar path for John Sarcone in the Northern District of New York, naming him first as the interim U.S. Attorney and then, when his interim term expired, naming him as the first assistant U.S. attorney and a “special attorney,” effectively designating him as the “Acting U.S. Attorney.”.

    It has been revealed that when challenges to the legitimacy of Chattah’s and Sarcone’s appointments followed, lower courts agreed that neither had been validly appointed. Sauer then came to the Supreme Court, where he told the justices that Chattah’s appointment was not only lawful, but “a critical tool that the Executive Branch has used without meaningful objection for 25 years.” He urged the court to take up that case, and to hold the New York case until the Nevada case is resolved.

    In a recent development, in addition to those disputes, the justices will consider three other noteworthy petitions for review on Dec. 4:.

    One thing to keep in mind: although the justices are slated to vote on these cases for the first time on Dec. 4, they may not act on any of them right away. In particular, for several years, the court has had a general practice of not granting a petition for review until the justices have considered it at two conferences. After the Dec. 4 conference, the justices will meet again on Dec. 11.

    Recent findings suggest that finally, yet another high-profile petition for review is likely to be before the justices soon: Trump v. Clinton, in which Trump is seeking to revive his lawsuit against Hillary Clinton (and several others, including the Democratic National Committee) alleging “a coordinated scheme … to undermine his candidacy and Presidency through fabricated accusations of Russian collusion.” Clinton originally waived her right to file a response to Trump’s petition, but the court called for a response, which she filed on Nov. 13. In her response, Clinton contends that “President Donald Trump and his attorneys” “attempt to frame a routine opinion disposing of a frivolous lawsuit as a threat to ‘the Presidency.’”.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    Which international thriller should you watch this weekend?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This month’s recommendations feature Zhang Yimou’s sumptuous story of organized crime in 1930s Shanghai; Sergei Loznitsa’s disturbing satire set in Russian-occupied Ukraine; and Manuella Martinelli’s quietly haunting depiction of Augusto Pinochet’s Chile.
    • With Gong Li (Memoirs of A Geisha, Farewell My Concubine) in the lead role as Bijou, a nightclub singer and the mistress of an underworld boss (Li Boatian), Zhang Yimou’s Shanghai Triad features opulent period sets and a propulsive narrative.
    • Over the course of seven days, Shuisheng learns about those rules as he witnesses gangland shootouts, discovers that Bijou is having an affair, and watches as Bijou’s relationship with the Boss unravels in intrigue and betrayal.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This month’s recommendations feature Zhang Yimou’s sumptuous story of organized crime in 1930s Shanghai; Sergei Loznitsa’s disturbing satire set in Russian-occupied Ukraine; and Manuella Martinelli’s quietly haunting depiction of Augusto Pinochet’s Chile.

    Glamorous, criminal underworld,1930s Shanghai.

    With Gong Li (Memoirs of A Geisha, Farewell My Concubine) in the lead role as Bijou, a nightclub singer and the mistress of an underworld boss (Li Boatian), Zhang Yimou’s Shanghai Triad features opulent period sets and a propulsive narrative. The story unfolds from the perspective of 14-year old Shuisheng (Wang Xiao Xiao) who has been sent from the countryside by his uncle to work for the Boss, who in turn makes him a personal servant to Bijou. “This is Shanghai,” Shuisheng is told. “There are hidden rules in everything you do or say.”.

    Over the course of seven days, Shuisheng learns about those rules as he witnesses gangland shootouts, discovers that Bijou is having an affair, and watches as Bijou’s relationship with the Boss unravels in intrigue and betrayal.

    Before making Shanghai Triad, Yimou and Li had previously collaborated on several classic films including Ju-Dou (1990) and Raise the Red Lantern (1991)—which is being re-released in theaters across North America for its thirty-fifth Anniversary.

    Directed by Zhang Yimou, 108 minutes.

    Streaming on multiple platforms.

    Recent findings suggest that composed of a series of several loosely linked vignettes that take place in Russian-occupied territory in Ukraine, and based on real-life amateur videos, Ukrainian director Sergei Loznitsa’s (The Two Prosecutors) Donbass makes you question everything you’re seeing. Up is down and right is wrong as actors get dressed to film what is supposed to be real news; a police chief explains to a man why his car no longer belongs to him; a bureaucrat at a maternity hospital shows staff a huge stock of food that they say they haven’t received.

    Loznitsa’s skills are on full display as he dips in and out of incidents with minimal set-up—you really don’t know where you’re headed, or what anyone will say or do—which is perhaps a good summary of what life was and is like in these zones.

    According to recent reports, filmed after Russia’s 2014 annexation of Crimea and its covert operations in the eastern Donbass region, but before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Donbass keeps you transfixed with its bewildering and inexorable logic. In that sense, it hits too close to home. Donbass isn’t out there. It’s right here, wherever home may be. We are all living in Donbass’s world of greed, corruption, and the perversion of truth.

    Directed by Sergei Loznitsa, 122 minutes.

    Streaming on multiple platforms.

    In preparation for Manuella Martelli’s gripping new film, The Meltdown (2026), which releases early next year, you should watch her directorial debut, 1976 (released in the US as Chile ’76). The two films are part of a planned trilogy that explores Augusto Pinochet’s dictatorship and its aftermath.

    Chile ’76 takes place three years after Pinochet seized power, overthrowing the democratically elected government of Salvador Allende—but none of that is top of mind for Carmen (Aline Küppenheim), a well-off middle-aged woman who heads out to her summer home to supervise renovations. In the course of her daily activities, Carmen witnesses incidents that give her pause—for instance, people on the street being dragged away—but since they don’t directly affect her, she moves on.

    When a priest asks Carmen to help care for a wounded young man, she slowly discovers what’s actually happening in her country. Chile ’76 doesn’t hit you over the head with lessons about authoritarian regimes and how they operate. Instead, it reveals how even well-meaning people can turn a blind eye to violence and repression…until they can’t anymore.

    Directed by Manuella Martelli, 96 minutes.

    Streaming on multiple platforms.
